# The 10 Best Running Shoes of 2026 — Fleet Feet Guide

Fleet Feet editors and gear testers (Tom Rivett, Mandy Wahl, Evan Matsumoto) tested hundreds of shoes to curate this list of the best running shoes for 2026. The guide emphasizes that there is no single "best" shoe for all runners; the right choice depends on foot shape, running style, cushioning preferences, and training goals. Testing incorporated real-world performance, weight, materials, durability, and data from over 5 million 3D foot scans.

## Top 10 Running Shoes of 2026

1. **ASICS GEL-Nimbus 27** — $124. Plush, protective cushioning; FF BLAST PLUS ECO foam; 8mm drop; 9.3 oz (W) / 10.8 oz (M). Best for long-distance runs and everyday training.
2. **Brooks Ghost 17** — $113. Nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 midsole; increased stack height; drop reduced from 12mm to 10mm; 8.9 oz (W) / 10.1 oz (M). Best for beginners and experienced runners alike.
3. **HOKA Clifton 10** — $116. Increased stack height with drop shifted from 5mm to 8mm; EVA foam; 8 oz (W) / 9.8 oz (M). Best for long runs, quick paces, and easy cruising.
4. **Karhu Ikoni 3.0** — $116. Designed using 3D foot scan data; removable sock liner; 8 oz (W) / 9.6 oz (M); 8mm drop. Best for everyday training and those who use orthotic inserts.
5. **New Balance Fresh Foam 1080 v14** — $124. Pillowy Fresh Foam X with ~3% bio-based content; 6mm drop; 8.3 oz (W) / 10.4 oz (M). Best for high mileage and hard efforts.
6. **Mizuno Wave Rider 29** — $113. Nitrogen-infused ENERZY NXT foam with MIZUNO WAVE structure; 10mm drop; 8.0 oz (W) / 9.3 oz (M). Best for neutral gait runners needing high mileage.
7. **On Cloudmonster 2** — $135. Double layer Helion superfoam with CloudTec cushioning; rocker shape; 5.5mm drop; 8.1 oz (W) / 10.4 oz (M). Best for tempo runs, long runs, and races.
8. **Saucony Ride 18** — $109. PWRRUN+ midsole foam; 8mm drop; 8 oz (W) / 9.1 oz (M). Best as a do-it-all everyday trainer.
9. **Altra Lone Peak 9** — $145 (trail shoe). Zero drop (0mm); 25mm/25mm stack; FootShape toe-box; MaxTrac outsole; 9.5 oz (W) / 11.2 oz (M). Best for trail running and hiking.
10. **Nike Air Zoom Pegasus 41** — $109. ReactX foam with two Air Zoom units (forefoot and heel); 10mm drop; 8.8 oz (W) / 10.4 oz (M). Best for versatile daily training and cross-training.

The guide also includes sections on best running shoes by brand, category, foot shape, and common FAQs (stability vs. neutral, pricing, mileage lifespan of 300-500 miles, and fit guidelines). Fleet Feet offers a 30-day Happy Fit Guarantee and free shipping/returns on orders over $99.

### What makes it the best?

During our runs with the Saucony Endorphin Speed 5, we found it to be a versatile trainer that has the power for faster runs, the comfort for longer mileage, and the flexibility for easier days. However, its combination of exceptional energy return scores in the lab, the use of a nylon plate, and the SPEEDROLL geometry makes it our top tempo running shoe.

The shoe immediately reacted when we wanted to pick up the pace. Our energy return results show it’s edging closer to super shoes, reaching 73.2% in the heel and 78.2% in the forefoot. Together with the SPEEDROLL geometry, we enjoyed its smooth yet strong forward momentum.

Another reason for ES5’s extra snap is the nylon plate in the midsole. What’s special about this type of plate is that it maintains flexibility. Our bend test verifies this with a pliability rating 16% above average, boosting both comfort and versatility.

**Category Winners:**

1. **Best Overall – adidas Adizero EVO SL (Score: 94)** – Features 100% Lightstrike Pro superfoam, ultra-light at 7.9 oz (223g), with 74.3% (heel) and 70.3% (forefoot) energy return, 5/5 breathability, and 36% more flexible than average. Best for neutral runners.

4. **Best Race – Nike Vaporfly 4 (Score: 93)** – Ultra-light at 5.6 oz (166g), 13% lighter than Vaporfly 3, with full ZoomX midsole, spoon-shaped carbon-fiber Flyplate, 18% stiffer than average, 4/5 breathability and durability. Best for 5K-21K distances.

Give the most thought to your daily trainer, because it’s the shoe that you’re going to spend the most time with. The miles will add up quickly, so prioritize not only a comfortable fit, but a smooth ride and good durability. Every runner, however, will have different preferences for those characteristics, so we’ve included a wide range of shoes that work best, whether you seek a bouncy and plush shoe or a firm and stable experience.

Our team of nearly 300 local runners and staff tested more than 100 new models to determine the best running shoes so far this year. After logging at least 100 miles in each pair, analyzing the data collected in our shoe lab, and reviewing hundreds of feedback surveys from our test team, these shoes stood out.

## R.A.D UFO

![Sport footwear featuring vibrant colors and unique design elements.](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/301a3fa2-4c7a-43df-9ad1-f49ba75bd9dc.jpg?crop=0.923xw:1xh;0.038xw,0xh&resize=980:* "Sport footwear featuring vibrant colors and unique design elements.")

Vomero. Glycerin. Those are a couple titans of comfort, but they’re also the [cushioned models](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a20865760/best-cushioned-running-shoes/) our testers most favorably compared to this bouncy, new, and shockingly fun trainer. It’s the first real running shoe from “Rally Against Destruction,” a company that got its start in CrossFit. The brand’s marketing efforts on social media are edgy and full of energy—and some curse words. That vibe carries over to the aesthetic of the shoe and, ultimately, the road feel.

One tester described these as her new favorite “sproing-sproing shoes.” Another tester, Sean O’Connor, a long-distance runner who has competed in backyard ultras, added, “The cushion on this shoe was amazing—so squishy and soft. I found myself grabbing this shoe on easy days and on long days because of its comfort. On my long runs of 20-plus miles, they were extremely comfortable the whole time, and my feet never felt tired.”

That comfort comes to you via a two-layer midsole made with a PEBA blend that R.A.D calls Supefoam. It’s further proof to my claim that you can make a killer trainer right now if you just tune a slab of PEBA and find a way to lash the foot down on top. Some of the [best running shoes](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a19663621/best-running-shoes/) lately have been seemingly the most simple.

But tuning this likely wasn’t so simple because this foam really wants to act like a pogo stick. Helping to control your flow is a mighty heel bevel and forefoot rocker. The two combine to give the shoes an extra bulbous shape. Surprisingly, it all works to help direct your motion forward.

## New Balance Ellipse

![New Balance Ellipse logo or design](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/3d6fa48f-9411-40dd-b059-23dbdfbd50d5.jpg?crop=0.923xw:1xh;0.038xw,0xh&resize=980:* "New Balance Ellipse logo or design")

With the release of the Ellipse, [New Balance](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a22590253/best-new-balance-shoes/) wanted to introduce a shoe that encapsulates the joyous feel of going on a group run. New Balance Senior Global Project Manager Paul Zielinski explained how they set out to create a shoe that matches the communal aspect of our sport. He described the shoe as a means to “stop thinking or stop worrying about the run, stop worrying about other things.”

The midsole is pillowy EVA-based Fresh Foam X. The New Balance team redesigned the geometry of this familiar foam to have a bounce-back compression that’s trampoline-like. But that spring is really just to put a jig in your step when running in a comfy cruiser. The Ellipse isn’t meant for speed sessions or racing; it doesn’t have a towering stack height (38 mm); and there’s no plate sandwiched inside to produce a propulsive snap. Ultimately, it is meant to be a vehicle for fun.

Our testers loved the cushioning and ride, comparing the Ellipse to a plush Hoka Bondi, only lighter and bouncier.

## Altra Experience Flow 3

![Running shoe designed for performance.](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/b8598042-e098-4a24-a6f8-87ebe74004f9.jpg?crop=1xw:1xh;0xw,0xh&resize=980:* "Running shoe designed for performance.")

It's been three years since [Altra](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a23311221/best-altra-running-shoes/) began releasing running shoes with a heel-to-toe drop. The formerly zero drop–only footwear brand wanted to give no-drop newbies a way to ease into its realm. And it seems to be the right move. Since our testers started running in Altra shoes with a 4mm drop—diehards and first-timers—they’ve rated the road and trail models highly. The Experience Flow 3, following in its predecessors’ footsteps, doesn’t disappoint.

“I enjoyed running in this shoe,” said Chris Greg, who’s familiar with Altra trainers. “The heel cushion was a bit more than other Altra shoes that I have worn before. It’s a great, happy medium between the heavy cushioning trend versus a neutral minimalist shoe. The forefoot of the shoe was highlighted by the traditional Altra wide toebox.”

For Tiffany Volpe, who’s tested for us since 2012, the Experience Flow 3 was the first Altra shoe she tried. She said it was worth the wait.

“I was so excited to try Altra finally!” she said. “Altra built its reputation on zero-drop shoes, and I really enjoyed the ‘low drop’ model. Altra packed the midsole with their foam to deliver a more responsive ride, without going overboard on softness. I’d describe the feeling underfoot as a nice blend of comfort and protection.”

## Asics Superblast 3

![Asics Superblast running shoes](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/cc5d1939-3d20-4025-b570-4ff380788468.jpg?crop=0.974xw:0.433xh;0.017xw,0.369xh&resize=980:* "Asics Superblast running shoes")

In just a few short years, the [Asics](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a22140215/best-asics-running-shoes/) Superblast became a fan favorite. The light and soft super trainer is remarkably versatile, able to cruise on a recovery jog as easily as it lets you stride out on more spirited efforts. The third version maintains that utility, but it is much softer and more fun right out of the box, thanks to a foam upgrade. Asics is now using the same Aliphatic TPU (A-TPU) foam, called FF Leap, found in its racing shoes like the Metaspeed Ray. That carbon-plated racer is darn near impossible to contain—it wants to go fast, and only in a straight line. But when you harness it, it’s a thrill. In the Superblast 3, you get that sensation, but without the unpredictable nature. Credit that to a few key features: a 10mm layer of FF Blast Plus on the bottom, a medial post–like bit of foam under the arch, and, frankly, a footprint that’s about as big as a 1970s Cadillac Fleetwood.

“The cushioning was extremely soft,” said sub-four-miler Colin Abert, who tests shoes for us in his postprofessional running life. “It helped to cushion impact significantly, so I felt like I could run really long distances in this shoe without feeling too beat up.”

The improved cushioning and response are most obviously felt in the forefoot, where Asics significantly boosted the “bounce pod,” a diamond-shaped protrusion that basically acts like a piston with each landing. To dial up the sensation even more, Asics carved a diamond-shaped groove onto the top of the FF Leap foam, so you feel its impact right under your foot.

## Diadora Atomo Star

![Sneaker with a vibrant yellow design positioned on a textured surface.](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/9350ccaa-900a-49e0-9a6c-68406e69cd12.jpg?crop=0.923xw:1xh;0.058xw,0xh&resize=980:* "Sneaker with a vibrant yellow design positioned on a textured surface.")

Diadora isn’t exactly a household name at American running stores—yet. The Italian brand has been quietly engineering a comeback, and the Atomo Star is its clearest statement of intent. Built around Anima N2 supercritical EVA foam and made in Italy, it’s a max-stack daily trainer with a balanced, protective ride that rewards patience over pace, but it still picks up beautifully.

The 6mm drop and pronounced heel bevel make for a smooth transition, and the wide base keeps things stable without drag. Anthony Dentino, who runs 40 miles a week at 6:45 pace and lands with a heel strike, found it dependable across both treadmill and road. “It’s comfortable and stable—I feel confident knowing it offers a smooth, durable ride,” he said. He would bench it for race day but called it more than capable for fartlek efforts and squarely at home on distance runs.

The microfiber and mesh upper feels premium, breathable, and secure without eating your heels or choking your midfoot, though Dentino noted the lacing didn’t lock down as snugly as other shoes he’s tested, which has been my experience as well. The Duratech outsole grips well on dry roads and treadmills alike—just note that the exposed midsole foam may be a liability in wet conditions.

## Adidas Hyperboost Edge

![A person running in athletic shoes on a concrete surface.](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/6cdb7e3f-1404-4ec8-af3a-be5b4d4d5f0d.jpg?crop=0.882xw:0.956xh;0.079xw,0xh&resize=980:* "A person running in athletic shoes on a concrete surface.")

[Adidas](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a22170339/best-adidas-shoes/) is modernizing its Boost foam with Hyperboost Pro, a lighter and livelier PEBA- based foam for daily training. By trapping air between pellets, the shoe sheds weight and blends the cushioning of the TPU-based Boost with the energy return of the TPE-based Lightstrike Pro. Comparable to the Asics Superblast or Saucony Triumph, the Hyperboost Edge is performance-driven yet tuned for everyday use.

The midsole delivers a responsive, energetic ride. It’s a versatile option for runners who want ample cushioning in a lightweight package. Testers praised the Hyperboost Edge’s seamless heel-to-toe cushioning. They noted that the shoe felt responsive when picking up the pace. “It’s energetic, fun, comfortable, and ready to turn even treadmill monotony into something a little more exciting and enjoyable,” said tester Dee Koutsourais.

## Nike Pegasus 42

![Pair of athletic shoes laid on a concrete surface](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/184d99c5-52c4-45cb-b8e5-1ac43ea4712d.jpg?crop=0.923xw:1xh;0.038xw,0xh&resize=980:* "Pair of athletic shoes laid on a concrete surface")

“The Pegasus was my shoe in high school,” said one wear-tester who is also a personal trainer and high school track coach. It’s a common refrain for many of us, as it’s been a budget-friendly workhorse trainer for more than four decades. It’s one of those shoes that’s going to work well for most runners, most of the time. So, with that kind of legacy, you don’t make big overhauls. But, for the newest Peg, [Nike](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a22843945/best-nike-running-shoes/) made a few big tweaks: new Air unit, new last shape, and cushioning that’s tuned based on shoe size.

The biggest headline is the one you don’t see. Taking learnings from the Pegasus Premium, Nike swapped out the two disconnected Air bags for a single, full-length unit. But it’s not just a flat slab in there. The Air unit is actually curved, much in the same scooped configuration of carbon-fiber plates—it sits closer to the heel but places more foam directly beneath the ball of your foot. The change allowed Nike to put 3 mm more foam under the toes without altering the overall stack height (37 mm thick under the heel). And that Air unit is now tuned differently as shoe size increases—the thinking is that bigger runners are served better by a thicker Air bag with higher pressure.

Even so, you won’t mistake this shoe for a max-cushioned trainer. It still has the relatively firm ride you’ve always found in the Pegasus, but it gets 15 percent more energy return. In a briefing with Nike’s product team to share in-depth details, they said the goal here is to “feel the ground, but not be on the ground.” That is, the shoe delivers enough cushioning but still responds quickly to your demands.

Above that, you may notice the shoe feels just a little roomier. That’s by design and makes the shoe a bit more democratic. Previous Pegs had a slightly cramped toebox, leading to a racy feel. But a new last that’s said to be “about 90 percent the same” provides more room at the pinkies and big toes, making more room for your forefoot. It also gets more toe spring—the upward curvature at the very front of the shoe—which our test team found helps to keep the shoe feeling propulsive.

# Runner's World Shoe Awards 2026 - Training Shoes

This article presents Runner's World's annual awards for the best training running shoes of 2026. Nearly 300 local runners and staff tested over 100 new models, logging at least 100 miles in each pair, to determine the winners. The article emphasizes that daily trainers are the most important shoes for runners, requiring comfort, smooth ride, and durability.

## Award Winners (16 shoes):

1. **R.A.D UFO** ($200) - Max-Cushioned Trainer, 8.9 oz (M)/7.5 oz (W), 8mm drop. First running shoe from CrossFit brand R.A.D. Features PEBA blend "Supefoam" midsole. Testers described it as "sproing-sproing shoes" with amazing squishy cushioning.

2. **New Balance Ellipse** ($145) - Neutral Trainer, 9.6 oz (M)/7.7 oz (W), 8mm drop. Pillowy Fresh Foam X with trampoline-like bounce. Not meant for speed; designed for fun, comfortable cruising.

3. **Altra Experience Flow 3** ($145) - Neutral Trainer, 9 oz, 4mm drop. Low-drop model from formerly zero-drop brand. Traditional Altra wide toebox with responsive cushioning.

4. **Asics Superblast 3** ($210) - Max-Cushioned Trainer, 8.4 oz, 8mm drop. Uses FF Leap (A-TPU) foam from racing shoes. Extremely soft and versatile. Downside: loud footfall.

5. **Diadora Atomo Star** ($250) - Neutral Trainer, 9.7 oz (unisex), 6mm drop. Made in Italy with Anima N2 supercritical EVA foam. Max-stack daily trainer with balanced, protective ride.

6. **Adidas Hyperboost Edge** ($200) - Max-Cushioned Trainer, 9.0 oz (M)/7.6 oz (W), 6mm drop. Modernizes Boost with lighter PEBA-based Hyperboost Pro foam. Energetic and responsive.

7. **Brooks Glycerin Flex** ($170) - Neutral Trainer, 9.4 oz (M)/7.3 oz (W), 6mm drop. Foldable design with diagonal flex zone. DNA Tuned foam with dual-cell nitrogen-infused technology.

8. **On Cloudmonster 3** ($130-$170) - Max-Cushioned Trainer, 10.4 oz (M)/8.5 oz (W), 6mm drop. Three layers of Cloudtec cutouts. Lively, controlled roll; excellent for long runs.

9. **Saucony Endorphin Azura** ($150) - Performance Trainer, 8.5 oz (M)/7.5 oz (W), 8mm drop. 40mm of PEBA-based Pwrrun PB foam, plateless. Speedroll rocker geometry.

10. **Mount to Coast C1** ($180) - Neutral Trainer, 9.2 oz (M), 6mm drop. CircleCell foam midsole. 42mm heel stack. Smooth heel-to-toe transition.

11. **Nike Pegasus 42** ($109-$130) - Neutral Trainer, 10.0 oz (M)/8.3 oz (W), 10mm drop. New full-length curved Air unit, roomier last, 15% more energy return.

12. **Anta PG7** ($100) - Max-Cushioned Trainer, 9.5 oz (M)/8.6 oz (W), 8mm drop. Budget-friendly max-cushioned trainer from Chinese brand. Peak Gravity cushioning.

13. **Asics Sonicblast** ($95-$180) - Performance Trainer, 8.7 oz (M)/7.5 oz (W), 8mm drop. FF Turbo² A-TPU foam with Pebax plate. 46mm stack (not World Athletics legal).

14. **New Balance 1080v15** ($170) - Max-Cushioned Trainer, 9.1 oz (M)/7.2 oz (W), 6mm drop. Complete overhaul with new Infinion foam (supercritical TPEE/TPU). Slightly firmer than previous versions.

15. **Nike Structure Plus** - Stability trainer with modernized-retro design. Features ZoomX foam and ReactX. Designed to make stability less boring.

16. **Puma Deviate Nitro 4** - Listed in jump-to menu but full review not included in excerpt.

<summary>
This is a comprehensive Wirecutter guide on how to choose the best running shoes, updated in 2025. The guide is written by Seth Berkman and is based on insights from eight experts (including physical therapists, podiatrists, a running coach, and shoe company executives), extensive research, and over 5,500 miles of testing by the Wirecutter team since 2017.

**Key Recommendations:**

- **Best Neutral Running Shoes:** Asics Novablast 5 (women's $130, men's $130) — versatile daily trainers with noticeable propulsion and bounce. Also recommended: New Balance 1080v15 and Nike Pegasus 41.
- **Best Stability Running Shoes:** Saucony Guide 17 (women's $100, men's $110) — a drastically redesigned trainer with ample cushioning. Also recommended: New Balance Fresh Foam X 860v14.
- **Best Low-Drop Running Shoes:** Altra Escalante 4 (women's $130, men's $130) — a zero-drop shoe with good cushioning and a comfortable toe box.

**Key Buying Advice:**

- **Fit is paramount:** Aim for at least a thumb's width of space between your longest toe and the end of the shoe, as feet expand while running.
- **Try many shoes:** Visit a specialty running store for a fitting. Try on multiple pairs and go back to the ones that felt best.
- **Comfort rules:** If a shoe feels off when you first try it on, it likely won't feel better on a run.
- **Shop with a goal:** Consider distance (cushioning) vs. speed (weight and responsiveness).
- **Neutral vs. Stability:** Start with neutral shoes. Only move to stability shoes if you feel you want more support or if a doctor recommends them. Experts note that overpronation is an overused term and most people fall in the middle of the pronation bell curve.
- **Heel-to-toe drop:** Traditional shoes have 10-12mm drop. Low-drop shoes (0-4mm) are an alternative for those who prefer a more natural feel, but should be eased into to avoid injury.
- **Sizing:** Be flexible — every brand's sizing is different. Use your normal size as a starting point but don't be afraid to size up or down.
- **Gender-specific shoes:** Not necessarily needed, though women's shoes typically have narrower heels and different width options. Focus on comfort features rather than gendered marketing.
- **Rotate shoes:** Having multiple pairs can prevent overuse injuries and allow cushioning to recover between runs.
- **Return policy:** Check return policies, especially when buying online.

**Testing Methodology:** The team tested over 100 pairs of shoes over seven years, with testers putting at least 50 miles on each pair. They evaluated cushioning, responsiveness, ride, ground feel, fit over time, sole and upper support, weight, and style.

URL: https://www.nytimes.com/wirecutter/reviews/best-running-shoes

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive Wirecutter guide on how to choose the best running shoes, updated in 2025. The guide is written by Seth Berkman and is based on insights from eight experts (including physical therapists, podiatrists, a running coach, and shoe company executives), extensive research, and over 5,500 miles of testing by the Wirecutter team since 2017.

**Key Recommendations:**

- **Best Neutral Running Shoes:** Asics Novablast 5 (women's $130, men's $130) — versatile daily trainers with noticeable propulsion and bounce. Also recommended: New Balance 1080v15 and Nike Pegasus 41.
- **Best Stability Running Shoes:** Saucony Guide 17 (women's $100, men's $110) — a drastically redesigned trainer with ample cushioning. Also recommended: New Balance Fresh Foam X 860v14.
- **Best Low-Drop Running Shoes:** Altra Escalante 4 (women's $130, men's $130) — a zero-drop shoe with good cushioning and a comfortable toe box.

**Key Buying Advice:**

- **Fit is paramount:** Aim for at least a thumb's width of space between your longest toe and the end of the shoe, as feet expand while running.
- **Try many shoes:** Visit a specialty running store for a fitting. Try on multiple pairs and go back to the ones that felt best.
- **Comfort rules:** If a shoe feels off when you first try it on, it likely won't feel better on a run.
- **Shop with a goal:** Consider distance (cushioning) vs. speed (weight and responsiveness).
- **Neutral vs. Stability:** Start with neutral shoes. Only move to stability shoes if you feel you want more support or if a doctor recommends them. Experts note that overpronation is an overused term and most people fall in the middle of the pronation bell curve.
- **Heel-to-toe drop:** Traditional shoes have 10-12mm drop. Low-drop shoes (0-4mm) are an alternative for those who prefer a more natural feel, but should be eased into to avoid injury.
- **Sizing:** Be flexible — every brand's sizing is different. Use your normal size as a starting point but don't be afraid to size up or down.
- **Gender-specific shoes:** Not necessarily needed, though women's shoes typically have narrower heels and different width options. Focus on comfort features rather than gendered marketing.
- **Rotate shoes:** Having multiple pairs can prevent overuse injuries and allow cushioning to recover between runs.
- **Return policy:** Check return policies, especially when buying online.

**Testing Methodology:** The team tested over 100 pairs of shoes over seven years, with testers putting at least 50 miles on each pair. They evaluated cushioning, responsiveness, ride, ground feel, fit over time, sole and upper support, weight, and style.
</summary>

# The Best Running Shoes For Every Type of Run

These are the top models we’re loving so far in 2020.

By [Runner's World](https://runnersworldonline.com.au/author/chelsea-brunckhorst/)

You know what you want from your running shoes: [light weight](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a20865752/best-lightweight-running-shoes/), [cushioning](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a20865760/best-cushioned-running-shoes/), [support](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a20865766/best-stability-running-shoes/), and a [comfortable fit](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a20865742/most-comfortable-running-shoes/). Of course, the most important part of any shoe is your experience over the hundreds of miles you’ll take them on. To help you find your next great pair, and to get a sense of how updates to your favorite road or [trail shoe](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a22115120/best-trail-running-shoes/) may change how it fits or performs, we review hundreds of [men’s](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a26028922/running-shoes-for-men/) and [women’s shoes](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a25578469/best-running-shoes-for-women/) each year. Scroll deeper for longer reviews of our top picks so far this year, a look at how we test and select these models, and helpful buying tips and insight from our gear experts.

### How We Test Shoes

*Runner’s World* has the most comprehensive shoe testing process in the industry. We work with more than 350 local runners of all ability, age, and size, for real-world wear-testing on paved roads, dirt paths, and rocky singletrack trails. After a month of running more than 100 miles, our testers report back their findings on features like fit, comfort, performance, and ride. While our testers are putting miles on the shoes, the same models undergo a battery of mechanical tests in our RW Shoe Lab, to objectively measure each shoe’s cushioning, flexibility, sole thickness, and weight. Our test editors combine their own experience in the shoe with data from the lab and feedback from our wear testers to create reliable, useful reviews of every shoe we run in.

![](https://rw2021prod.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/why-trust-us-rw-composition2-1568991038.jpg)

In addition to running hundreds of miles in each test model, we measure shoes in our lab and cut apart shoes to see how they’re constructed.

### Does a Shoe’s Cushioning Matter?

Some runners care a lot about weight, and research shows that you expend more aerobic energy with heavier shoes. Lighter shoes typically have less cushioning, which can make them feel faster, but new midsole foams now make a plush feel possible without adding much heft to the shoe. [If you’re going long distances](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a26860886/long-distance-running-shoes/), some extra cushioning might be a better option, as it provides impact absorption.

To test its softness, our Shoe Lab takes individual measurements in both the heel and forefoot, since the overall experience can vary based on where a runner touches down and toes off. The cushioning scores are given on a scale of 1 to 100, with one being the firmest. (A harder-feeling shoe won’t necessarily lack cushioning, and [according to some biomechanical research](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0125196), a too soft midsole can actually increase peak impact forces.) In addition to those key stats, we also look at the shoe’s stability features, flexibility, and energy return to help you find one you’ll love.

DNA Loft is Brooks’s softest cushioning.

Adidas’s Boost foam keeps its bounce no matter how cold it is outside.

## **What Does “Drop” Mean?**

A [shoe’s drop](https://www.runnersworld.com/news/a20826073/does-a-shoes-heel-to-toe-drop-matter/)—sometimes referred to as offset—is the difference between the heel and the forefoot measurements, or how much your toes “drop” below your heel. It’s important because a higher drop can lead to more heel striking and also transfers some strain away from the lower leg and up toward the knee. Conversely, a lower offset will shift that load farther down the chain of motion during your gait cycle to the calf and Achilles. Neither option is necessarily better than the other; when deciding on a shoe’s drop, choose what feels most natural and comfortable to you, taking into account your personal running mechanics and injury history. Many shoes have a drop between 8 and 12 millimeters, but some shoes have less than 6mm. A few based on minimalist designs have zero drop.

Altra’s Rivera has an equal heel and forefoot stack height, which translates to zero-drop.

In contrast, Brooks’s Trace has a 12mm heel-to-toe drop.

## FAST

---

### Hoka One One Carbon X2

---

**Weight: 238g (M), 198g (W)  
Drop: 5mm**

---

A year ago, the [Carbon X](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a27495253/hoka-one-one-carbon-x/) had us going fast over mid- to long-distance runs, but after our wear-testers clocked hundreds of miles, we determined that midfoot-strikers got the most out of the shoe. A heel-to-toe roll propelled by the early-stage Meta-Rocker (Hoka’s tech that slightly curves the sole for a rocker motion) felt quite aggressive to some testers, especially heel-​strikers. Those runners won’t feel left out with this update, though. A protruding heel, which is similar to [Hoka’s TenNine](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a31250883/hoka-one-one-tennine-trail-shoe-review/) (though not as massive), absorbs shock and provides stability for runners who touch down on the back of their foot. “If I raced a marathon or less, I’d go with the [Saucony Endorphin Pro](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a32844327/saucony-endorphin-pro-first-look/),” said a heel-​striking tester. “If I raced a 50K or more, I’d use the Carbon X2.” As a heel-striker and tester of the Endorphin Pro, I agree. As in the Endorphin Pro and Hoka’s other racing shoe, the Rocket X, a carbon-fiber plate in the midsole promotes quick and snappy transitions. The X2 feels hardy for longer mileage, as well as versatile enough for speed training. Our test team liked the refined upper—the reinforced lacing and engineered support zones made it feel  
more secure.*—Test Editor Amanda Furrer*

---

### **Saucony Kinvara 12**

---

**Weight: 212 g(M), 184g (W)  
Drop: 4mm**

---

The 12th version is a fantastic homecoming for the Kinvara. The 11 felt stiffer and heavier than its predecessor, and we got fairly strong “daily trainer” vibes from the super-plush tongue and thick upper. The 12, however, nudges the Kinvara back toward its racing roots. It’s a touch lighter and much more flexible, like the shoe’s early models, with a snug midfoot and new blend of Pwrrun foam. Saucony tweaked the foam’s mix of EVA and polymers to boost energy return, and while it doesn’t pack the punch of the brand’s Endorphin series, it does feel firmer and more responsive. A slim layer of softer TPU-based Pwrrun+ sits on top to keep the shoe comfy as a daily trainer—long runs included. That keeps it lightweight and speedy, yet able to withstand a ton of miles. “All in all, the versatile cushioning has made the Kinvara my go-to shoe,” one tester said. “Whether I’m going short or long, going out for a leisurely run or for speedwork and hills, this shoe is game.” Just don’t look too long at the exposed foam outsole—it’s sufficiently grippy for dry road running, but gets dirty and looks worn after a few miles.*—Test Editor Morgan Petruny*

---

## SOFT

---

### **Brooks Glycerin 1**8

---

**Weight: 289g (M), 255g (W)  
Drop: 10mm**

---

In a past life, the Glycerin may have been relegated to recovery runs, but it’s gradually metamorphosed into an everyday, every-run workhorse. Proof lies in our most recent testing, when wear-testers raved about the 19’s versatility, wearing the shoe for both long runs and speedier efforts. We found we were reaching for the Glycerin more often than the ever-popular (and award-winning) Brooks Ghost. The most appealing feature is the shoe’s DNA Loft midsole, which makes the trainer softer than earlier models without sacrificing energy return. The ride feels smooth and bouncy instead of squishy, as one might expect from Brooks’s most-cushioned shoe. Testers who were nursing injuries found the Glycerin’s cushioning supportive and helpful in rebuilding their base. But softness is not sequestered to the midsole alone; the bootie-like interior provides surrounding comfort. However, you might want to size up before making a commitment. The shoe felt quite snug, and testers reported a mix of minor discomforts, from a slightly cramped toebox, to rubbing at the Achilles, and a too-narrow midfoot that caused pins and needles. But nail the size and your feet will feel like they’re cradled in springy memory foam.*—A.F.*

---

### Asics EvoRide 2

---

Weight: 235g (M), 195g (W)  
Drop: 5mm

---

Looking for a shoe that gives you a snappy turnover for half marathons or tempo runs at 10K pace? The EvoRide 2 may be it, thanks to its FlyteFoam midsole and GuideSole geometry. Asics uses a lightweight and noticeably firm midsole foam, but it is protective enough for lightweight runners at quick speeds. Testers appreciated that the foam feels consistent along its entire length—some shoes tend to be squishier under the heel or forefoot. “I immediately liked the amount of spring,” said one female tester who runs 30 miles per week at 7:45 pace. “It felt responsive with fast strides, not like a marshmallow that absorbed energy.” Some of that is attributable to the shoe’s GuideSole feature, which basically gives it an exaggerated round shape underfoot to help it roll more smoothly from heel to toe-off. (You’ll find the same extreme toe spring on the beefier [MetaRide](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a26572278/asics-metaride/) and GlideRide models, but the EvoRide is the fastest of the trio.) Those underfoot features are the same ones found on the debut version, but Asics improved the upper on this one. The most obvious fix is the tongue, which was ridiculously thick and plush a year ago. The update is just thick enough to reduce lace pressure and wraps comfortably over the top of your foot.*—J.D.*

---

## STABLE

---

### Brooks Launch GTS 8

---

Weight: 249g (M), 229g (W)  
Drop: 10mm

---

You’re not wrong if you thought “GTS” stood for “Go-To Shoe.” This year, [Brooks](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a20866339/best-brooks-running-shoes/) is simplifying its naming convention by pairing stability shoes to its neutral siblings and tacking on GTS—now redefined as “Go-To Support.” The next Transcend and Bedlam, for example, have been named the Glycerin GTS and Levitate GTS. And, in the case of the Ravenna, it’s now being called the Launch GTS—a light stability shoe that’s speedy like the neutral Launch. Testers appreciated the comfortably firm cushioning and found Brooks’s holistic guide-rail system (firm foam along the medial and lateral sides of the heel serve as bumpers to align the knee and ankle) supportive. The most noticeable revamp—besides the name—is the new air mesh upper. Testers liked that it was light and breathable, yet some wished for a more traditional padded heel collar instead of the oddly shaped one here. “It felt to me that the heel collar was too high on my ankle,” said a tester, “and it rubbed my lateral ankle bone, causing discomfort.”*—A.F.*

---

### Saucony Guide 14

---

**Weight: 297g (M), 266g (W)  
Drop: 8mm**

---

Saucony’s versatile stability shoe now looks race-ready with 3D-print overlays adorning the engineered-mesh uppers, and sharing the same color scheme of the racier Kinvara. The Guide has plush padding in the heel collar and gusseted tongue. This stability version of Saucony’s Ride has a lightweight TPU medial post and sturdy heel counter to lend support, which testers found comfortably supportive. One tester even had a revelatory moment wearing the shoe. “I often lean toward more cushioned shoes with the assumption that, being a ‘curvier’ runner, the weight striking the hard surface was the cause of some injuries,” she said. “The Guide gave me some cushioning, but the shoe’s stability helped fix my pain.” This shoe is still soft, though, thanks to Saucony’s Pwrrun midsole, combined with a top layer of Pwrrun+. The latter is composed of a lightweight foam that promotes a springier step while absorbing impact.*—A.F.*

This is a Runner's World Australia/New Zealand webpage featuring an article titled "The Best Running Shoes For Every Type of Run." The article reviews top running shoe models, explains how Runner's World tests shoes (using over 350 local runners who run 100+ miles per month, plus mechanical lab tests measuring cushioning, flexibility, sole thickness, and weight), and provides a guide to understanding shoe features like cushioning, drop/offset, and stability.

Key shoe reviews include:

**FAST category:**
- **Hoka One One Carbon X2** (238g M, 198g W, 5mm drop) – Carbon-fiber plate, improved heel design for heel-strikers, versatile for speed training and longer races.
- **Saucony Kinvara 12** (212g M, 184g W, 4mm drop) – Lighter and more flexible than v11, new Pwrrun foam blend, returns to racing roots.

**SOFT category:**
- **Brooks Glycerin 18** (289g M, 255g W, 10mm drop) – DNA Loft midsole, versatile for everyday runs, bootie-like comfort but runs snug.
- **Asics EvoRide 2** (235g M, 195g W, 5mm drop) – FlyteFoam midsole, GuideSole geometry for smooth roll, improved tongue from v1.

**STABLE category:**
- **Brooks Launch GTS 8** (249g M, 229g W, 10mm drop) – Light stability shoe with guide-rail system, new air mesh upper, but odd heel collar design.
- **Saucony Guide 14** (297g M, 266g W, 8mm drop) – TPU medial post for stability, Pwrrun+Pwrrun+ midsole, race-ready look.

The page also includes navigation to other Runner's World categories: Training, Mental Health, Nutrition & Weight Loss, Running Shoes & Gear, Beginners, News, and Runner's Stories.

This Runner's World UK video from 1 May 2025, presented by Ali, reviews five of the best beginner running shoes for 2025. It first explains that running shoes fall into two categories: neutral shoes (for normal pronation) and stability/support shoes (for overpronators). Key fitting tips include going half a size up from lifestyle shoes, prioritizing comfort, and ensuring a thumb's width of space between the toes and shoe tip. The recommended shoes are daily trainers (versatile allrounders), priced £130–£165.

The five picks are:
1. **Nike Pegasus 41** – A classic, moderate-stack daily trainer (34mm heel/24mm forefoot) with React X foam and Air Zoom units. Solid and dependable, suitable for most runs but less ideal for very fast intervals.
2. **Adidas Supernova Rise 2** – A firm, stable, old-school-feel shoe offering connectedness and control. Excellent value, similar to the Pegasus as a dependable workhorse.
3. **Asics Novablast 5** – Bouncy and versatile with max cushion (40.5mm heel/32.5mm forefoot) using FF Blast Max foam. Fits wider in the midfoot, good for heel strikers, and handles easy runs through tempo efforts.
4. **Brooks Glycerin 22** – Premium (£165) comfort-focused shoe with DNA Tuned midsole (larger cells in heel for cushioning, smaller cells in forefoot for pop). Wider last for stability; livelier than previous versions.
5. **New Balance Fresh Foam X 1080 v14** – Softest pick but not mushy, responsive, with a new engineered mesh upper and added rubber outsole. Good for high-mileage training and marathons. Note: sizing may run small, so consider going up a full size.

# Runner's Word UK: Best Road Running Shoes for Summer/Autumn 2025

This is a transcript of a Runner's World UK podcast episode (published 29 Sep 2025) where the team discusses 18 top road-running shoes tested over the past few months. The shoes are categorized by type and use case.

## Daily Trainers
- **Adidas Boston 13** (£140, 255g): Speed-leaning daily trainer with a firm, stiff ride. Moderate stack height, 6mm drop. Good for runners who prefer a firmer feel.
- **New Balance FuelCell Rebel v5** (£140, 255g men/180g women): More cushioned than the v4, now better suited for long runs. 6mm drop. Described as a versatile daily trainer, though slightly less snappy than the v4.

## Speed & Versatile Trainers
- **Adidas Adizero Evo SL** (£130): Very versatile, responsive cushioning without being overly squishy. Jack of all trades. Can handle everything from easy runs to 5k/10k races.
- **Brooks Ghost 17** (£135): Staple daily trainer, perfect for beginners or those wanting guaranteed comfort and stability.
- **Puma Velocity Nitro 4** (£110, 10mm drop): Excellent value daily trainer. Wide toe box, more traditional ride with less pronounced rocker. A refreshingly less maximalist feel.

## Super Shoes
- **New Balance SC Elite v5** (£260): Completely redesigned from v4 — more nimble and aggressive. 8mm drop (up from 4mm). "Probably the most normal looking super shoe."
- **Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 3**: 95g lighter than predecessor. 3.6% more economical than Nike Alphafly 3 per scientific testing. Very narrow, aggressive forefoot. Rachel ran a 2-minute PB in it at London Marathon.
- **Nike Vaporfly 4**: Lighter than ever. Best for 5k to half marathon. 35mm heel stack. Less cushioning than some competitors, so maybe not ideal for full marathon.
- **Tracksmith Eliot Racer**: Unique design with foam above the plate. Very soft footbed, comfortable. Premium aesthetic. Expensive.

## Performance/Race Shoes
- **Saucony Endorphin Speed 5**: Nylon plate (not carbon). Good first step into plated shoes. Versatile — can be used for easy runs, tempos, progression runs. More stable than carbon racers.
- **Hoka Rocket X3** (£220): Fast with a great rocker. Good for larger runners (tested by an 87kg reviewer). Performance-oriented.
- **ASICS Metaspeed Edge/Sky Tokyo** (~170g): Edge for cadence runners, Sky for stride runners. Very bouncy, responsive. New foam combination. Edge is a favorite for marathon distance.

## Stability Shoes
- **Saucony Guide 18**: Modern stability without heavy medial posts. Different density foams and guide rails. Good daily trainer for those needing support.
- **Saucony Hurricane 25** (£165): Max cushion stability shoe. Very comfortable for easy/recovery runs.

## Max Cushion & Recovery
- **ASICS Mega Blast** (£210): Uses new FF Turbo Squared foam. Very bouncy — "the shoe does a lot of the work for you." Less stable than Super Blast 2.
- **Brooks Hyperion Max 3** (£170, 6mm drop): Nylon plate, DNA Gold foam. Sharp geometry, pushes you along. Great for easy runs and progression runs.
- **Nike Vomero Plus** (£155): Uses ZoomX foam (same as Vaporfly/Alphafly). Very soft and smooth. Wide platform, stable. Built as a recovery shoe but can handle faster paces.

We are determined to help you find your next favorite pair of shoes and running gear—and let you know the stuff you should stay away from. Creating authentic, trustworthy reviews of shoes and running gear is at the core of everything we do at *Runner’s World*.

## Why Trust Us?

For more than 50 years, *Runner’s World* has helped runners of all levels find the best new gear to improve their runs. Our wear-test team includes former collegiate athletes, a few sub-3:00 marathoners, an ultrarunner who completed a 255-mile race in the Swiss Alps, and a crew who runs nearly every day at lunchtime. ## The Shoe Lab

Every shoe test begins with mechanical measurements in the RW Shoe Lab. We weigh every shoe and take measurements of the heel and forefoot thickness (stack heights) so you know exactly what the heel-to-toe drop is for your favorite shoe. Then we use precise scientific equipment to measure cushioning, energy return, and flexibility. That gives us a complete picture of each shoe, so we can compare it to the thousands of other models we’ve tested—and verify or dispute manufacturer claims. We’re the only running shoe reviewers who test shoes in a lab.

![Image no longer available](https://media.hearstapps.com/loop/runners-world-shoe-testing-67659bee689af.mp4/poster.jpg)

Our impact testing allows us to determine a shoe’s energy return.

Every shoe also gets road or trail tested by our local team of nearly 300 wear-testers. We have at least six runners (usually twice that many) run in each shoe for at least 100 miles over the course of a month before sharing insights into how the shoes performed. At the same time, our staff runs in each pair to personally observe each shoe under real-world conditions.

## Staff and Expert Testing

For other categories, like tech and accessories, we devise tests to measure battery life, lumens of headlamps, breathability of fabrics, and more. When we can’t test a product, we’ll let you know. args.summary: This is a Runner's World webpage explaining how the publication tests and reviews running gear, primarily shoes. The testing process involves two main components: mechanical lab testing (the RW Shoe Lab) and real-world wear-testing. In the lab, every shoe is weighed, measured for stack heights and heel-to-toe drop, and tested for cushioning, energy return, and flexibility using scientific equipment. This is supplemented by road/trail testing from a team of nearly 300 wear-testers who run at least 100 miles in each shoe over a month, along with staff testing. The team tests over 150 pairs of shoes annually, plus GPS watches, wireless earbuds, recovery tech, and apparel. The staff includes a Runner-in-Chief (Jeff Dengate), Test Editors (Amanda Furrer, Morgan Petruny), a Senior Video Producer (Pat Heine), a Director of Content Hype (Aly Ellis), a News Editor (Theo Kahler), a Senior Editor for Commerce (Cat Bowen), and a Senior Photographer (Trevor Raab). The page also describes categories tested: Shoes, Gear (shorts, bras, socks, etc.), Tech & Equipment (headphones, smartwatches, treadmills), and Training (gels, foam rollers). Annual awards include Shoe Awards and Gear of the Year. The publication includes an affiliate disclosure stating they earn commissions on some product links but that does not influence coverage. Runner's World+ members can apply to become shoe testers.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: The 15 Best Running Shoes of 2026, Tested by Runner's World ---
URL: https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a19663621/best-running-shoes

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Runner's World published "The 15 Best Running Shoes of 2026," featuring top picks from over 300 testers. The article is organized by categories: Training, Racing, and Trail shoes. Key selections include:

**Best Training Shoes:**
- **Best Overall:** Adidas Adizero Evo SL ($150) – Lightstrike Pro foam, 7.9 oz (M), 7mm drop, 39mm stack. Praised for responsive cushioning, lightweight versatility, and ability to handle daily training, speedwork, and long runs. Cons: tongue can shift, wide midfoot for narrow feet.
- **Best Value:** New Balance Ellipse ($145) – Fresh Foam X cushioning, bouncy trampoline-like ride, 9.6 oz (M), 8mm drop, 38mm stack. Available in multiple widths. Cons: bulky, not for speedwork.
- **Best Daily Trainer for Narrow Feet:** Brooks Ghost 18 ($150) – Nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3, 10.2 oz (M), 10mm drop, 36mm stack. Soft, responsive, beginner-friendly. Cons: potential hot spots in bunion area, runs hot, stiff initially.
- **Best Daily Trainer for Wide Feet:** Brooks Glycerin 23 ($175) – DNA Tuned midsole, 10.6 oz (M), 8mm drop, 38mm stack. Wide accommodating fit, great for long runs. Cons: slightly stiff in forefoot.
- **Best for Long Runs:** Nike Structure Plus ($170) – Stability road shoe, ReactX + ZoomX foams, 10.8 oz (M), 10mm drop, 42mm stack. Max-cushioned with built-in support. Cons: some found it cumbersome.
- **Best for Race Training:** Hoka Clifton Pro ($165) – Supercritical EVA, Meta-Rocker, 10.4 oz (M), 8mm drop, 42mm stack. Great for long runs without a plate. Cons: foam less responsive than some supercritical foams, narrower fit.
- **Best for Shock Absorption:** New Balance 1080v15 ($170) – New Infinion foam (supercritical TPEE/TPU), 9.1 oz (M), 6mm drop, 39.9mm stack. Softer, more responsive than previous versions. Cons: too much shoe for some college-aged testers.
- **Best for Run/Walking:** On Cloudmonster 3 ($190) – CloudTec sole, 10.4 oz (M), 6mm drop, 35mm stack. Firm underfoot with rocker profile. Cons: heel collar could be softer.
- **Best for Stability:** Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 ($155) – Guide rails system, DNA Loft v3, 10.6 oz (M), 10mm drop, 37mm stack. Increased cushioning, versatile for overpronators. Cons: testers wanted longer laces.
- **Best for Recovery:** Hoka Bondi 9 ($175) – Max cushioning, 10.5 oz (M), 5mm drop, 43mm stack. Extremely plush, 10mm thicker stack than Bondi 8. Cons: heavy, not for fast runs, narrower fit.

**Best Racing Shoes:**

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive Wirecutter guide on how to choose the best running shoes, updated in 2025. The guide is written by Seth Berkman and is based on insights from eight experts (including physical therapists, podiatrists, a running coach, and shoe company executives), extensive research, and over 5,500 miles of testing by the Wirecutter team since 2017.

**Key Recommendations:**

- **Best Neutral Running Shoes:** Asics Novablast 5 (women's $130, men's $130) — versatile daily trainers with noticeable propulsion and bounce. Also recommended: New Balance 1080v15 and Nike Pegasus 41.
- **Best Stability Running Shoes:** Saucony Guide 17 (women's $100, men's $110) — a drastically redesigned trainer with ample cushioning. Also recommended: New Balance Fresh Foam X 860v14.
- **Best Low-Drop Running Shoes:** Altra Escalante 4 (women's $130, men's $130) — a zero-drop shoe with good cushioning and a comfortable toe box.

**Key Buying Advice:**

- **Fit is paramount:** Aim for at least a thumb's width of space between your longest toe and the end of the shoe, as feet expand while running.
- **Try many shoes:** Visit a specialty running store for a fitting. Try on multiple pairs and go back to the ones that felt best.
- **Comfort rules:** If a shoe feels off when you first try it on, it likely won't feel better on a run.
- **Shop with a goal:** Consider distance (cushioning) vs. speed (weight and responsiveness).
- **Neutral vs. Stability:** Start with neutral shoes. Only move to stability shoes if you feel you want more support or if a doctor recommends them. Experts note that overpronation is an overused term and most people fall in the middle of the pronation bell curve.
- **Heel-to-toe drop:** Traditional shoes have 10-12mm drop. Low-drop shoes (0-4mm) are an alternative for those who prefer a more natural feel, but should be eased into to avoid injury.
- **Sizing:** Be flexible — every brand's sizing is different. Use your normal size as a starting point but don't be afraid to size up or down.
- **Gender-specific shoes:** Not necessarily needed, though women's shoes typically have narrower heels and different width options. Focus on comfort features rather than gendered marketing.
- **Rotate shoes:** Having multiple pairs can prevent overuse injuries and allow cushioning to recover between runs.
- **Return policy:** Check return policies, especially when buying online.

**Testing Methodology:** The team tested over 100 pairs of shoes over seven years, with testers putting at least 50 miles on each pair. They evaluated cushioning, responsiveness, ride, ground feel, fit over time, sole and upper support, weight, and style.
</summary>

*Editor’s note: we continuously monitor and update our rankings on this page when new running shoes are released – the list was last updated on 12th June 2026.*

Looking for the best running shoes reviewed by experts? We’ve tested hundreds of running shoes across every category — daily trainers, long-run cushioners, race-day super shoes, and trail runners — to bring you our definitive rankings.

A few years ago, you could get away with one or two pairs that kinda did everything. Now, thanks to leaps in shoe tech, your shoe rack should probably looks like a training plan – something for [easy days](https://marathonhandbook.com/best-daily-running-shoes-reviewed/), something for [workouts](https://marathonhandbook.com/best-running-shoes-for-workouts/), and then you probably want a dedicated pair of coveted [race day carbon-plated supershoes](https://marathonhandbook.com/best-carbon-plate-running-shoes-reviewed/).

And honestly, that’s a good thing. The tech in running shoes has exploded. Midsoles are lighter, foams are bouncier, and the variety means you can find something that fits your stride perfectly.

We’ve tested **hundreds of pairs** across every category – we’ve linked to our YouTube reviews below – and narrowed them down to **the best of the best** running shoes, the shoes that actually deliver on their promises. Whether you’re chasing a PR, jogging easy miles before sunrise, or hammering out intervals at the track, this guide has you covered.

Below, you’ll find our picks for **the best daily trainers**, **the best super shoes**, and **the best workout shoes** on the market right now. Each one has been **road-tested, ranked, and reviewed with brutal honesty**, because if a shoe isn’t fun to run in, what’s the point?

A quick clarifier: ‘workout shoes’ are sometimes called ‘super trainers’; they’re this relatively new category of shoe designed for your speed sessions, your [threshold workouts](https://marathonhandbook.com/threshold-run-guide/), your [long runs](https://marathonhandbook.com/splitting-long-runs/). They’re more aggressive than a daily trainer, but more forgiving than a race day shoe.

So without further ado, what follows is the cumulation of every running shoe review we’ve done in the past 12 months: here are the greatest running shoes money can buy right now, for any use case.

## #**5 Best for value: [Puma Velocity Nitro 4](https://www.amazon.com/Velocity-Nitro-Running-Silver-Medium/dp/B0FR5L1JRR?crid=15OF8PXLPZECN&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.KAcDGULRI-DVwkEX6uH1tjsmBKFAmoeA7Scift8czNm9E_MQO02U_G90DIKwQtMsTfSH-IrRSfGo8sxEzQlvuEBzu3X_NNgjrbai0MG5rD2b3FjLGcCkztRxrx20J7E8rmHZaGWYGwEzwTrhJ3cbUi--WMk9Ji8olq8YkeYJYgspHc7WYSE7d6uuAs6L9uGTV0i1sxgkmC_z5ZwhgOagrM4bm1CyhMzXt578eqfzMAi0uUOmbBrPrgJ7p-INEYa9Se3Iaa5OalDzl0cm_99prtK3tiMBkbut1pTb0HMiMgc.AUbAJQDvdDnHe3D97Seq2T5tj6wnZKuvQEfOEBrvs3I&dib_tag=se&keywords=Puma%2BVelocity%2BNitro%2B4&qid=1759607864&refresh=1&sprefix=puma%2Bvelocity%2Bnitro%2B4%2Caps%2C504&sr=8-3&th=1&psc=1&linkCode=ll1&tag=marathonhandb-20&linkId=4218b2330d65fb80b4944e9aadf172df&language=en_US&ref_=as_li_ss_tl)**

### Score: 8.1

This isn’t Puma’s most cushioned easy running shoe. The Magnify Nitro 3 is probably better protection for your feet. But I find the Velocity Nitro 4 to be the best. A big reason for that is that the entire midsole is made out of **Puma’s supercritical Nitro foam**, which is an upgrade from previous versions of the Velocity.

This makes the shoe light and fast and fun to run in, but still supportive enough for an easy running shoe. And as a bonus, when brands switch to full supercritical foam, the price usually jumps, **but this shoe stayed relatively cheap.**

At first glance it feels flimsy because it’s quite flexible, and the stack height of 36 mm is small these days. But it has a tightly packed heel and **the traction is really good**. If you’re running in slippery areas, this is probably a good shoe for you.

We gave it an overall rating of 8.1. It gained a lot of points on value, given that it’s so affordable. It lost some points on comfort because the toe box is a little small.

The Velocity Nitro 4 is for you if you like to feel the ground under you, if traction matters, and if you like a bit of pop on easy days.

Stay away from it if you’ve gotten used to the big, chunky feel of today’s high-stack shoes—it feels smaller. And if durability is your main concern, this isn’t bad, but because it’s so flexible you’ll probably run through it faster than some of the bulkier shoes.

### Score 8.5

The Nimbus is kind of a nightmare for these power rankings because it’s a bit of a boring shoe and I’ve mentioned it so many times already. But it’s also impossible to ignore. **The Nimbus is ASICS’s perennial easy running shoe**, and it’s been around almost as long as I have.

It’s heavy, it has no aspirations to be a workout shoe, but it does its one job very well: **it takes you through many comfortable, easy miles**. I’ve yet to meet a person who dislikes the Nimbus. When beginners ask me which shoe to buy, I usually point them to the Nimbus because it’s probably the safest shoe in the world.

The Nimbus 27 actually came with some key updates: **a bit more supercritical foam in the midsole** (lighter and bouncier), **more traction on the outsole,** and **it’s the tallest Nimbus yet**—while still lighter than the Nimbus 27.

We gave it an overall score of 8.5, with the value score being the highest. Not because it’s cheap, but because it lasts so long it’s worth the money.

Buy the Nimbus if you’re risk-averse about running shoes, if you like traditional-feeling trainers with some new tech updates, and if you value durability. Avoid it if you want something faster on easy days or if you want a marshmallow-soft feel like a Hoka Clifton. The Nimbus is comfortable, but the midsole is more firm than soft.

## #**5 Best Shoe For Easier Paces:** **[Hoka Skyward X 2](https://www.runningwarehouse.com/HOKA_Skyward_X_2/descpage-HSKY2M1.html?&from=mratnhd)**

### Score: 8.5

What you’ll notice with super shoes is that some are more geared for speed workouts, and others are more so made for long runs. The Skyward X2 is the latter. It’s a big, bulky, incredibly protective and durable shoe — especially for Hoka, which in the past has had some issues with the durability of their shoes.

The Skyward X2 is built different. It’s got 49 mm of stack height, making it one of the tallest shoes in the world. And that huge midsole is made of two foams: a PEBA foam up top for responsiveness, and a supercritical EVA at the bottom for stability and durability.

What I like about this shoe is that it’s a huge improvement from the Skyward X1, which was a massively weird shoe to put on the market back in 2024. When I tried it for the first time, it was big, tall, a little wobbly, and quite heavy. This shoe is lighter than its predecessor, and also importantly, it’s more stable. The carbon plate is shaped to give you forward propulsion, but also lateral stability — which is important when you’re 50 mm above ground.

Now, use cases for the Skyward X2: it’s not a fast interval shoe. It is a lot of material to carry around. But it’s excellent on long runs, even fartlek runs, and importantly, it can handle an easy run. I really like my super trainers to handle different paces. There are some super trainers I left out of this list because they’re so uncomfortable to run easy in. The Skyward X2 can kind of do everything.

We gave it an overall score of **8.5**. Top marks for design. Props to the Hoka designers for making this shoe two years ago and breaking the mold a little bit — it was one of the very first super trainers on the market. And the two I really like because it dials in the problems that the one had. The one was too heavy, the one was too wobbly. This shoe takes care of both problems.

## **#4 Best Shoe For Versatility And Durability: [Adidas Hyperboost Edge](https://www.runningwarehouse.com/adidas_Hyperboost_Edge/descpage-ADHBEM2.html?&from=mratnhd)**

### Score 8.5

I didn’t see this shoe coming. Adidas had a problem inside of their shoe offering. They had super top-level racing shoes, especially seeing the success of the Pro Evo 3 on the feet of Sabastian Sawe and Yomif Kejelcha. And then on the other side of the spectrum, they have what might be the most popular shoe in the world in the Evo SL. I don’t really call that shoe a super trainer because it doesn’t quite have the power that all these shoes that I’m about to present have. What Adidas was missing was a powerful shoe that could handle your fastest workouts. And the Hyperboost Edge is pretty much that.

This shoe looks pretty simple, and it’s made of two parts. One part I like, and one part that I don’t.

What I really like is the midsole, called Hyperboost Pro. It’s a supercritical pellet-based foam that’s very responsive, very stable, and as far as I can tell, very durable as well. I’ve really enjoyed this shoe for workouts. I can run fast in it. I can run easy. It can handle a whole lot of different paces. Doesn’t hurt that the midsole looks good and doesn’t look too funky — I feel like I can wear this out and look kind of stylish. Maybe you be the judge on that.

But then on top of the midsole is the part that I don’t like. The upper is weird. It’s called Prime Weave, and it’s thick. It’s seemingly heavy, and it’s not that comfortable on the foot. So, disclaimer with this shoe: when I first put it on, my first couple runs, I developed a little blister over my Achilles tendon on both of my feet. Over time, that callused and went away, and now I don’t have any issues with the shoe. But still, in this day and age, you wouldn’t expect that to happen.

If not for the upper, this shoe would probably rank higher on my list. So clearly it lost marks in comfort, but we still gave it an overall score of **8.5**. Its performance score really helped it here. I just love how it feels and how it moves. I think it’s actually my favorite shoe to wear on this list, but wearing it kind of comes at a cost. So it’s my number four. A version two of this has the potential to become my favorite shoe with a better upper.

## **#3 Best Shoe for Long Runs:** **[On Cloudmonster 3 Hyper](https://www.runningwarehouse.com/On_Cloudmonster_3_Hyper/descpage-O3CMHM7.html?&from=mratnhd)**

### Score: 8.6

This is more of a speed-power super trainer than a cushioned and comfortable super trainer. The Cloudmonster Hyper series has always been speed-power, and this one is faster and more powerful than the previous.

To understand what’s going on with the Cloudmonster, we need to understand what’s going on with On. The brand is going through a not-so-subtle aesthetic change. We’ve come to know On as the shoe with tiny little cloud pods in its midsole. Those pods seem to be good for comfort, maybe even durability, but not so much for speed. So On’s fastest shoes seem to be slowly phasing those pods out. That’s what’s happening with the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper.

Instead of only having a half slab of supercritical foam like its predecessor did, this shoe has an entire slab from heel to toe, making it quite a bit faster. It still doubles with one layer of those Cloudtec pods to increase its stability and even durability, but in general, it feels a lot more like a super shoe than it does a daily trainer.

To me, the Cloudmonster is a bit too aggressive for easy runs, but I like it for long runs, for fartlek runs, and especially threshold runs — because it does have so much pop at the toe without being a full-on racing shoe.

I’ve also heard some complaints about comfort. Some people don’t like how the shoe feels on their feet. That hasn’t been the case for me. I’ve actually found the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper to be very comfortable. Maybe my favorite On shoe of all time, actually. So I gave it a pretty high rating in comfort and also performance.

The one drawback on this shoe is that it’s pretty pricey. **$220 is almost as much as a super shoe.** It will last you a long time, and it does feel good on the feet, but you could probably find something cheaper.

## **#2 Best Shoe for Power Without Compromising Comfort:** **[Brooks Hyperion Max 4](https://www.runningwarehouse.com/Brooks_Hyperion_Max_4/descpage-B4HYXM1.html?&from=mratnhd)**

### Score: 8.9

I’m especially a fan of this shoe because it represents a big revamp from Brooks. Not that the 4 is that different from the 3, but it’s solidifying Brooks as a brand that’s able to make not only light shoes and comfortable shoes, but powerful running shoes. And a couple years ago, that’s exactly what they were lacking.

The Hyperion Max 4 has three (actually four) components that I really like. The midsole is made of three parts: a DNA Gold PEBA foam up top, a supercritical EVA at the bottom for stability, and in the middle, a SpeedVault nylon plate. So not carbon — a little bit more forgiving, but still stiff enough to give you some pop. And on top is an upper that’s quite a bit more comfortable than most uppers we see in super trainers. So Brooks managed to find that balance between fast and aggressive and comfortable. I think it’s important for them to keep their shoes comfortable, because that’s kind of their trademark.

My one gripe with this shoe: somehow it’s the heaviest shoe on the list. **I cannot believe that a shoe as big as the Skyward X2 is not heavier than the Brooks Hyperion Max 4.** Brooks not only blew up their light shoes, they really gave them muscle — and it’s almost getting to be on the verge of too heavy, but it’s not there yet.

I love doing long runs in the Hyperion Max 4. I’ve done threshold runs, and I’ve even done hills, and those have felt good. It’s tough to make a big, powerful shoe that still feels good on the turnover, and I feel that Brooks has done that here.

Obviously, big points on design and comfort. **Overall score: 8.9.** I think this would have been the shoe of the year if not for our winning brand and our winning shoe’s magical release — I don’t think I can top number one. But this is clearly Brooks’s best super trainer to date.

## Honorable Mentions

A few quick honorable mentions before we move on to number one. I have two main ones here: the **Brooks Glycerin Max 2** and the **ASICS Magic Speed 5**. The only reason that neither of these shoes has made it onto this list is that both exist too far on one side of the spectrum.

The Glycerin Max 2 is very comfortable and really fun to wear, but it doesn’t really have enough teeth to compete with these other shoes. You can run easy in this shoe. You can do a good long run. But as soon as you pick it up for a threshold, it feels like it’s missing a beat. That’s why I didn’t rank it in my top five. But the comfort of the shoe made it close.

And then the Magic Speed 5. I love this shoe. I do a lot of workouts in this shoe. I did not include it because it’s so aggressive that it almost feels like a racing shoe more than a workout shoe. And I’ve heard from a lot of people that they don’t find that this shoe has enough support to really be a workout shoe. So I kind of counted it more as a racing shoe, even though I know it’s for workouts. Anyway, maybe this is a call to action for people who like a stiff, fast running shoe for workouts to check out the Magic Speed 5, because I really like the shoe.

![Youtube video](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='480'%20height='360'%20viewBox='0%200%20480%20360'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

 

---

## **#1 Best Shoe overall:** **[ASICS Superblast 3](https://www.runningwarehouse.com/ASICS_SUPERBLAST_3/descpage-AS3SB1.html?&from=mratnhd)**

**Need shoes for running too?** See our picks for the [best running shoes](https://marathonhandbook.com/best-running-shoes-reviewed/) overall, the [best marathon running shoes](https://marathonhandbook.com/best-marathon-running-shoes/), and the [best carbon plate running shoes](https://marathonhandbook.com/best-carbon-plate-running-shoes-reviewed/) for race day.

### Score: 9.0

I’ve been a big Superblast fan since the 2. I challenged myself to find a shoe that I liked more, and I failed.

Here’s what’s cool about the Superblast. **It’s the comfiest shoe on this list, but it’s also the lightest.** It has a unique set of qualities that are hard to find in another shoe.

The Superblast’s secret weapon: ASICS took its FF Leap foam — their aTPU supercritical foam that they use in their racing shoes like the Metaspeed Ray — and put it inside of their super trainer’s midsole. Now, some people fear that it would make the shoe not all that durable, because that foam is known to not last that long. This has not been my experience. I have several hundreds of miles run in this shoe, and so far we’re doing fine. I think it was a brilliant move to put that really good foam inside of that shoe.

The drawback: it makes this shoe expensive. Like most super trainers on this list, you’re paying a premium to run in the Superblast 3. The bonus, and what they don’t want to tell you, is that that makes the Superblast 2, if you can find it, much cheaper than it used to be. So if you can get your hands on a pair of Superblast 2s, go for it. The changes are not that huge, but if you compare the two, the Superblast 3 still wins.

I would say the key quality of this shoe is that **it feels good at every speed**. You can very much run an easy run in this shoe. You can pick it up and go up to threshold pace. You can run a fartlek and feel good. You can even do hills and feel all right. On the spectrum, it’s more on the protection-and-support-and-stability side than it is on the speed-power side, but I’m starting to feel that you may not need a carbon plate in your super trainers. My own thoughts on this are evolving. We’ve talked about it on recent podcasts: should you have a carbon plate inside of your super trainers? That’s a whole other kettle of fish. But for now, I’ve become a big fan of the Superblast 3, and I bet you will too.

**We ranked it at 9 out of 10.** Good marks across the board. Value is the only knock, really, on the Superblast. Overall, it scored a tiny bit higher than our other shoes here, but it was close.

Since our last power ranking, this shoe slid from position three to five because a couple really cool shoes hit the market. But I was still very impressed by the Endorphin Elite 2.

Saucony hadn’t really been as big a player in the world of super shoes as I would’ve expected, especially given they were one of the first companies to develop a super shoe back in the 2017–2019 era.

The standout feature of this shoe is the **midsole**, which is incredibly bouncy. I’ve been calling this one of the best shoes in the world since early this year, even before it started getting much attention. Very few pros were wearing them at major marathons, very few pros are sponsored by Saucony. But that changed at the World Championships when Uruguay’s María Pía Fernández won a surprise bronze medal in the women’s marathon wearing the Endorphin Elite 2. We docked some marks for **comfort**. The downside of a squishy foam is there’s not much stability for pronators. I’m a pronator, not enough to wear stability shoes, but enough that I noticed some soreness in odd places after workouts. My feet tend to drift inward in these, and the foam doesn’t do much to stop that. It wasn’t enough for me to ditch them, I still love using them, but it’s something to be aware of.

This webpage from Marathon Handbook (updated June 12, 2026) provides expert-ranked reviews of the best running shoes across three categories: daily trainers, workout shoes (super trainers), and race day super shoes, based on hundreds of miles of testing by Senior Gear Editor Alex Cyr.

**Top Daily Running Shoes:**
1. ASICS MegaBlast (Score: 8.7) - Best overall daily trainer. Features FF Turbo 2 foam, 45mm heel stack, 7.5oz weight, very light yet cushioned. Can do easy runs and pick up pace. $225.
2. Nike Vomero 18 (Score: 8.6) - Best for responsiveness. ZoomX supercritical foam, bouncy and durable, 44mm heel stack, 11.5oz. $155.
3. Brooks Glycerin 22 (Score: 8.6) - Best for cushioning. Fully supercritical DNA foam, 38.5mm heel, 10.2oz. Felt flat after ~700km. $165.
4. ASICS Nimbus 27 (Score: 8.5) - Best for durability. Perennial easy running shoe, tallest Nimbus yet, 44mm heel, 11.3oz. Very safe beginner shoe. $175.
5. Puma Velocity Nitro 4 (Score: 8.1) - Best for value. Full supercritical Nitro foam, 36mm heel, 8.6oz, good traction. $140.

**Top Workout Shoes (Super Trainers):**
1. ASICS Superblast 3 (Score: 9.0) - Best overall. Comfiest and lightest on the list (8.8oz), FF Leap foam, 45mm heel. Excels at all speeds. $270.
2. Brooks Hyperion Max 4 (Score: 8.9) - Power without sacrificing comfort. DNA Gold PEBA foam + SpeedVault nylon plate, 46mm heel, 10.1oz. $200.
3. On Cloudmonster 3 Hyper (Score: 8.6) - Best for long runs. Full slab of supercritical foam, 39.5mm heel, 9.6oz. Fast and powerful. $220.
4. Adidas Hyperboost Edge (Score: 8.5) - Versatile and durable. Hyperboost Pro midsole, 45mm heel, 9oz. Upper caused blister issues. $200.
5. Hoka Skyward X 2 (Score: 8.5) - Best for easier paces. 49mm stack (one of tallest), PEBA + EVA foam, carbon plate, 10oz. $225.

**Top Race Day Super Shoes:**
1. Adidas Adios Pro Evo 2 - Best overall.
2. Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 - Best for your next PR.
3. Asics MetaSpeed Tokyo Edge & Sky - Best for a firm, light ride.
4. Adidas Adios Pro 4 (Score: 8.4) - Best for durability. More stable than Endorphin Elite 2.
5. Saucony Endorphin Elite 2 (Score: 8.0) - Best for cushioning. Very bouncy midsole, 39.5mm heel, 7oz. Stability issues for pronators. $290.

The page also includes shoe comparison guides (e.g., Hoka Clifton vs Bondi, Brooks Glycerin vs Ghost) and tech specs (stack height, weight, drop, MSRP) for each featured shoe.

## Who should buy

The Brooks Ghost 18 is a great match for:

* Long-time Ghost fans who want the same familiar ride, fit, and overall experience they've enjoyed for years.
* Heel strikers looking for a comfortable and easy-to-run-in daily trainer with proven durability and a stable feel.
* Casual runners who want one shoe for running, walking, travel, and everyday wear.

## Who should NOT buy

We think that runners looking for a bouncy and energetic ride will be disappointed by the Ghost 18. Brooks still uses the same DNA Loft v3 foam, and we found in the lab that it delivers below-average rebound. If you want a daily trainer that feels more lively and responsive, we believe the [PUMA Velocity Nitro 4](https://runrepeat.com/puma-velocity-nitro-4) is a better choice.

 

We also do not recommend the Ghost 18 for runners who want the highest level of cushioning possible. In our view, the [Ghost Max 3](https://runrepeat.com/brooks-ghost-max-3) is the obvious pick inside Brooks, while the [Nike Vomero 18](https://runrepeat.com/nike-vomero-18) is another excellent alternative.
