This shoe is going to be all good for things like that. And then my third like, durability and stability. Because of the quite firm foam you're getting with the Pegasus 42 and the relatively low stack, the stability is really good with this one. You can corner with confidence here, which is what some people are going to really appreciate. The Pegasus has always have a bit of a reputation for good durability, absolutely no reason why that's going to change now. This shoe is going to last for a long amount of time. But as we always say here on the channel, because I bought these shoes 100% with my money, we can now move on and bring you those all-important dislikes. The first one has to be that ReactX midsole. It's very overly firm and pretty lifeless for running in all honesty, which is that classic Pegasus we've come to expect in recent years. It really is now one of the slowest options out there on the market. An old, firm ride, no response, really no bounce, no cushion, no assistance really at all when you are trying to pick up the pace. Again, it's going to be fine for someone that just wants to jog a couple of 5Ks a week and wants a nice-looking shoe for their casual, for the gym, a nice durable and stable option as well. But for a more inspiring ride, for an up-and-coming runner that's really trying to take their running quite seriously, trying to progress their running, you really got to be looking elsewhere. We'll come on to those options later on in the video. The second dislike, it's obviously pretty heavy still as well. In an era where shoes are getting lighter and lighter, the Pegasus seems to be going the other way. Again, perfectly fine for that casual runner that just wants to do a few runs at a pinch, but as I keep saying, there are so many better options out there. My third dislike, personally, I wouldn't want to run a long distance in this shoe. So, for me, anything over 60 minutes, 75 up to about 90 minutes absolute maximum for me. There's just nowhere near enough cushioning. It's not going to look after your legs very well over the course of that long run. So, as I keep saying, if you do want some more dedicated running options, let's compare this to some of the bigger shoes out there on the market right now. The first one being the Asics Novablast version 5. The Novablast 5 is coming in around about £5 more expensive, 5 mm more stack, 2 mm less drop, 55 g lighter. The Novablast has got a little bit more foam underneath it and a lot less ground contact feel than the Pegasus 42. The Novablast foam is a lot softer, it's more cushioned. You're getting a much softer ride with that one versus the more firm ride in the Pegasus. The Nike's going to be a little bit better for that durability if you're looking for a daily shoe to really last a long time, but the Asics is going to be a faster option, it's going to be more fun, it's going to be better at a wide variety of paces. Nike wins in that stability area, but Asics is softer and more responsive for sure. Between the two, I'm definitely going to be picking the Novablast. Right, moving on to the all-conquering Adidas Evo SL. Evo SL is the same price as the Nike shoe, 2 mm more stack, 3 mm less drop, weighs a whopping 90 g less for me in my sizes. Now, I should start out by saying these shoes are very different. There's really not a direct competitor for the Pegasus shoe, but the whole world just utterly adores the Evo SL, and whatever shoe I review, I have to compare it to the Evo SL. So, I'm doing it for you guys down in the comments. The Evo SL is a lot softer than this one, way more responsive, way more bouncy, and a lot faster, too. A lot, lot faster than the Pegasus. It's also more unstable, which is where the Pegasus will be a lot better. The Pegasus is going to give a calmer, much more predictable ride, which some might prefer for their daily runs. Whereas the Evo SL is going to be a better option when you need something for those faster days, those tempo runs, those threshold runs, those interval sessions, and a much better race day option as well. The Evo SL isn't going to be the best jogging around shoe given its instability. So, again, the Pegasus might be a better option to go for there. But of course, the Evo SL is going to be much more fun for me. I'm definitely going to be picking the Evo SL between the two. Next up, let's compare it to the Puma Velocity Nitro version 4. The Puma's £20 cheaper here. We can regularly find that shoe for a lot less than RRP. 1 mm less stack, same drop, and 75 g lighter. See a bit of a theme here? Everything is lighter than the Pegasus 42. Puma have put their Nitro foam into this one, which is a little bit lighter and definitely a little bit softer. Still quite firm by 2026 standards, but a lot softer than the Pegasus shoe. Wider-footed runners are only better suited by the Pegasus, just a lot more room up front in the standard shoe, and particularly good to get that wider-footed option as well. Puma don't offer that, and it does run a little bit narrow. For me, I'd personally be picking the Velocity Nitro, just one of the best value daily options out there at the moment. Right, finally, let's move on to chat about Nike's own Vomero 18. The Vomero 18 is coming in at £5 more expensive, but I think that's going to be £5 well spent. It's got 9 mm more stack, the same drop, but a little tiny bit heavier. The Vomero range of shoes that Nike make are their more higher stack range of running shoes. So, the Vomero is a little bit softer, it's more plush, it's more bouncy, it's more responsive, and it has that dual layer mid-sole as well. So, you're getting the same ReactX that you're getting in the Pegasus, but on top of that, you're getting a half layer of Nike's ZoomX mid-sole, which is a lot softer and most crucially, a lot more bouncy and responsive as well. Most runners are going to be a much better served by the Vomero 18 that want to stay in the Nike brand. So, go with the Pegasus if you're looking for a more old-fashioned ride, prefer a little bit more ground contact feel in your running. Otherwise, the Vomero really wins out in every other way, in my opinion. So, would I buy this shoe again? What's my conclusions and final thoughts on Pegasus version 42? It's very easy to sit here and pick apart the shoe and say it's just not very good for running. It's going to get a lot of hate online, but also a lot of love as well. A lot of people really love the Pegasus and they never want it to change. The internet will always be divided with this one. The Pegasus line has changed and evolved quite a lot over the years. It's still as dependable as ever, comfortable as ever, durable, and a really nice stable option as well. For a lot of people, I think myself included, it really is now a lifestyle shoe that you can go out and get a few runs done in when you want to, rather than a dedicated running shoe. That's where the Vomero comes in. As I say, a lot of people looking for a Nike running shoe, definitely go with the Vomero range. If you like version 41, then I'm pretty sure you're going to like version 42 as well. It definitely rides a little bit better than the outgoing 41, but at the end of the day, just go with what you can get the best deal on and the colorway that you like. But, my TLDR on the Nike Pegasus 42 is a simple, no-fuss option, will no doubt be appearing in an outlet store near you soon, which a lot of people will appreciate. The next video coming up will be the Nike Vomero full review. Check that video out up here. And also, a video that YouTube thinks you're going to like just down there. I'll see you over there very soon. Let me know your thoughts on the Pegasus 42. Are you going to be getting it? Let me know down in the comments. If you're running it, let me know as well and help out the community. That's it, guys. Keep on working hard. Keep on getting done. I'll see you very soon in the next one.

## Nike Pegasus 42 Review (Ben Parkes, 14 Apr 2026)

**Main Topic:** A comprehensive, honest, and unsponsored review of the Nike Pegasus 42 daily running shoe, comparing it to key competitors.

**Key Changes from Pegasus 41:**
- Full-length curved Air Zoom unit (vs. separate front/back units in v41) – adds slight energy return but makes the shoe stiffer and 10g heavier.
- Slightly wider forefoot/toe box, new mesh upper, new outsole (slightly less rubber coverage).
- Same ReactX foam (firm), same stack height (37mm heel), same 10mm drop, same price (£130 UK, $5 more in USA).
- Weight: 357g (UK size 12) – notably heavy vs. competitors.

**Likes:**
1. Dependable and predictable – a consistent, reliable daily trainer.
2. Very comfortable upper with good breathability, lockdown, and padding; suits heel, midfoot, and forefoot strikers.
3. Excellent durability and stability due to firm foam and low stack; corners well.

**Dislikes:**
1. ReactX midsole is overly firm, lifeless, and unresponsive – one of the slowest options on the market.
2. Relatively heavy in an era of lighter shoes.
3. Insufficient cushioning for runs over 60–75 minutes (up to 90 min max).

**Competitor Comparisons:**
- **vs. Asics Novablast 5:** Softer, more cushioned, 55g lighter, faster and more fun. Pegasus wins on stability and durability. Reviewer picks Novablast.
- **vs. Adidas Evo SL:** 90g lighter, much softer, more responsive, faster. Pegasus is more stable and predictable. Reviewer picks Evo SL.
- **vs. Puma Velocity Nitro 4:** £20 cheaper, 75g lighter, softer. Pegasus better for wide feet. Reviewer picks Velocity Nitro.
- **vs. Nike Vomero 18:** 9mm more stack, slightly heavier, dual-layer midsole (ReactX + ZoomX), softer, more plush, more responsive. Reviewer says Vomero wins out for most runners wanting a Nike shoe.

**Final Verdict (TLDR):** A simple, no-fuss lifestyle shoe that can handle a few runs. Dependable, durable, comfortable, and stable – but lacks the responsiveness and cushioning of modern competitors. For dedicated runners, the Vomero 18 is a better Nike option. Likely to appear in outlet stores soon.

# Nike Pegasus 42 Review: A Versatile Workhorse

By [Caroline Bermel](https://www.fleetfeet.com/authors/caroline-bell-1)

The combination of ReactX foam and the responsive Air Zoom Unit gives the Nike Pegasus 42 a distinct feel that’s both familiar and fun underfoot. ​​

![The Nike Pegasus 42](https://cdn.fleetfeet.com/a:2.4-f:cover-w:1440/assets/NIKE-Pegasus-42-Chalk-Tattoo-Orange-Bright-Pulse-Violet-W-2_260327_103901.jpg?s=7688f5c2)

*All shoes are reviewed by the Fleet Feet tester team, which represents a wide variety of goals, foot shapes, running locations and terrains. Reviewers pound the pavement, climb the hills, tackle the trails, then come together to compare notes. Debates ensue over the feel of the cushioning, the purpose of the shoe, and how it compares to last year’s model. While each reviewer has their own individual preferences, we hope that capturing our debates will help you make an informed decision.*

The first time I put on the Nike Pegasus was the first time I fell in love with a running shoe. It wasn’t the brand-new 42nd version, it was the Pegasus 35. Light grey at the top and light pink at the bottom, it was the coolest looking pair of running shoes I had ever worn. I had just started working as an Outfitter at Fleet Feet Delray Beach and was discovering that running shoes are meant to be enjoyed, not just tolerated. Of course, this lesson was largely due to finally being fitted for the proper shoes.

As years went by, I branched out and explored other brands and models. When I returned to later iterations of the Pegasus, it didn’t spark that same joy in me. Some of them felt firm and clunky, a far cry from the smooth, flexible and springy sensation I experienced in the 35.

[Mason](https://www.fleetfeet.com/blog/meet-the-fleet-feet-reviewers#block-6382924) and I were excited to get our hands on the Pegasus 42, since Nike promised this latest version would be more responsive, lighter weight and better-fitting than the last. What’s the verdict? Read on to find out.

## Tech Specs

![The Nike Pegasus 42](https://cdn.fleetfeet.com/a:1.5-f:cover-w:1440/assets/NIKE-Pegasus-42-White-Metallic-Silver-Lapis-Total-Orange-M-6_260327_104222.jpg?s=c51baa3c)

## Nike Pegasus 42: The Feel

The Pegasus is a winged horse in ancient Greek mythology that symbolizes speed. The Pegasus franchise has often been described as a “workhorse” of a shoe, one that can log all kinds of miles through multiple training cycles, which is a more accurate equine comparison in my opinion.

First, Nike increased the toe spring, the upward curvature of the forefoot that guides you into your next stride. This shift makes it even easier to transition into toe-offs as soon as you land, for a smooth, fluid ride.

Nike also upped the ante with their proprietary Air Zoom Unit. These units host tensile threads that act as springs, contracting as you land and popping up as you take off. Previous versions of the Pegasus only had Air Zoom Units in the heel and forefoot. Shifting to a full-length unit delivers more of this springy surface area, delivering more energy return with every step.

I mentioned that the Pegasus 42 hasn’t broken any world records, and that’s because it’s not designed to be a racing shoe. The Pegasus encases the Air Zoom Units in ReactX midsole foam, adding some stability to the hyper-responsive ride. In Nike’s top-tier racing shoes, [like the Alphafly 3](https://www.fleetfeet.com/blog/nike-alphafly-3-review-worth-the-hype?srsltid=AfmBOoos6UDah9VJMzihRTMdCqIyRTtahjnjUj_khCd2FvzCgoa7u7xa), the Air Zoom Units are exposed. When the Air Zoom technology is encased in foam, the energy doesn’t have anywhere to go, so the energy return feels much more contained — as opposed to being completely exposed and able to bounce you down the road towards your next PR!

“The Pegasus 42 isn’t a flashy shoe, but it’s consistent and quietly impressive across just about any type of run,” says Mason. “It certainly isn’t a boring option either — the Air Zoom Unit works wonders to make the experience feel lively. This shoe is a bit of a “sleeper” option in my mind, like a sporty Honda Civic that’s hiding a big ol’ turbo charger under the hood.”

While I wasn’t chasing any PRs during my test runs in these, I did feel light and nimble on my feet. These shoes feel really versatile, and I can see runners enjoying them for easy runs and speedwork. However, that means they don’t excel at any one thing. They’re a “Jack of all trades, master of none” type shoe.

Mason agrees, saying, “After several runs, I found myself really appreciating the simplicity of the Pegasus 42. It’s a true “no frills” trainer in the best way, it just wants to rack up miles. Easy runs, long runs, walks and even some quicker strides all felt well within its comfort zone. Despite being a slightly lower profile trainer, there was always enough cushioning and structure for my feet once fatigue started to set in.”

## Nike Pegasus 42: The Fit

![The Nike Pegasus 42](https://cdn.fleetfeet.com/a:1.5-f:cover-w:1440/assets/NIKE-Pegasus-42-Chalk-Tattoo-Orange-Bright-Pulse-Violet-W-14_260327_104328.jpg?s=e8a36fe9)

The main update to the fit of the Pegasus is a wider forefoot. This makes the shoe more accommodating for those with wide feet, or those who just enjoy some extra wiggle room for their toes.

“This version of the Pegasus seems to have changed in the “fit and feel” department for the better,” Mason says. “The fit is true to size with no tightness or pressure points, and the upper materials feel more premium than I expected — both in hand and on foot. It’s one of those step-in experiences that immediately gives me confidence in a running shoe.”

I don’t have wide feet but my left foot is a C width, which is slightly wider than medium width for women (which is B). So, while I don’t wear a wide size, I won’t say no to extra toe space. I think the Pegasus 42 will be perfect for those types of runners and walkers.

A lightweight mesh upper feels soft yet secure, while a slightly tapered heel collar ensures my achilles will stay blister-free. I have narrow heels, and I found myself needing to tie the [marathon loop](https://www.fleetfeet.com/blog/how-to-lace-your-running-shoes-for-a-more-comfortable-fit#block-4942903) to reduce slippage. Otherwise, the ankle collar would be way too wide on me. For my fellow narrow-heeled cohorts, this shoe has extra eyelets around the ankle so you can do just that.

Not sure about the width or shape of your feet? Your best bet will be to head into your [local Fleet Feet](https://www.fleetfeet.com/locations). Fleet Feet outfitters use [3D fit id® foot scanning technology](https://www.fleetfeet.com/fit-process) to gather information about your feet and the support they need by taking precise measurements of your foot length, width and arch height. You can learn a lot about your feet while you’re there!

## How does the Nike Pegasus 42 compare?

![The Nike Pegasus 42](https://cdn.fleetfeet.com/a:1.5-f:cover-w:1440/assets/NIKE-Pegasus-42-Chalk-Tattoo-Orange-Bright-Pulse-Violet-W-20_260327_104456.jpg?s=53fa1240)

We took a look at some comparable models to see how the Nike Pegasus 42 stacks up. Here’s what we found.

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Tech Specs** | **Nike Pegasus 42** | **New Balance Ellipse v1** | **Altra Experience Flow 3** |
| Weight | 8.6 oz (W), 10.5 oz (M) | 7.6 oz (W), 9.6 oz (M) | 7.5 oz (W), 9 oz (M) |
| Stack height | 37 mm/27 mm | 37.9 mm/27.9 mm | 30 mm/26 mm (W),  32 mm/28 mm (M) |
| Heel-to-toe drop | 10 mm | 10 mm | 4 mm |
| Experience | Springy | Springy | Smooth |
| Price | $145 | $145 | $145 |

The Pegasus 42 and [Ellipse v1](https://www.fleetfeet.com/blog/new-balance-ellipse-v1-review-the-future-of-new-balance) are both categorized as “springy,” meaning they offer slightly more pep than your average trainer without being a full-blown “speed” shoe – this would require a carbon or nylon plate, per our categorization chart.

I found both shoes to feel remarkably similar, with almost identical stack heights.

For reference, a shoe’s stack height is the difference in height between your feet and the ground. Nike’s ReactX foam and New Balance’s Fresh Foam X foam both deliver a satisfying blend of softness and responsiveness, with the Ellipse feeling slightly more forgiving and the Pegasus more tuned for faster efforts.

[The Altra Experience Flow 3,](https://www.fleetfeet.com/blog/altra-experience-flow-3-review-smooth-miles-ahead) on paper, doesn’t appear similar to the other two shoes, but I couldn’t help but come back to it as a comparable option. Altra’s EGO™ P35 foam delivers that same hint of energy disguised under a soft step-in feel.

## Who is the Nike Pegasus 42 best for?

![The Nike Pegasus 42](https://cdn.fleetfeet.com/a:1.5-f:cover-w:1440/assets/NIKE-Pegasus-42-White-Metallic-Silver-Lapis-Total-Orange-M-15_260327_104532.jpg?s=0f9f4d0e)

The Nike Pegasus 42 is best for runners and walkers who like a balanced blend of cushioning — not too soft, not too firm. It’s what I call a “Goldilocks shoe.” It’s *just right.*

With its responsive Air Zoom unit, propulsive toe spring and steady, stable foam, the Nike Pegasus 42 can handle multiple kinds of runs. Whether you’re running easy, running long or running fast, this shoe can handle the pace and distance, making it a great bang for your buck at $145.

“I think the Pegasus 42 is an especially strong option for runners who want to experience that iconic “Nike” ride — the combination of ReactX foam and the responsive Air Zoom Unit gives it a distinct feel that’s both familiar and fun underfoot,” says Mason.

With a roomy toe box and accommodating ankle and heel collar, it will work best for runners and walkers who enjoy some extra space.

The guide is written by Seth Berkman and is based on insights from eight experts (including physical therapists, podiatrists, a running coach, and shoe company executives), extensive research, and over 5,500 miles of testing by the Wirecutter team since 2017.

**Key Recommendations:**

- **Best Neutral Running Shoes:** Asics Novablast 5 (women's $130, men's $130) — versatile daily trainers with noticeable propulsion and bounce. Also recommended: New Balance 1080v15 and Nike Pegasus 41.
- **Best Stability Running Shoes:** Saucony Guide 17 (women's $100, men's $110) — a drastically redesigned trainer with ample cushioning. Also recommended: New Balance Fresh Foam X 860v14.
- **Best Low-Drop Running Shoes:** Altra Escalante 4 (women's $130, men's $130) — a zero-drop shoe with good cushioning and a comfortable toe box.

**Key Buying Advice:**

- **Fit is paramount:** Aim for at least a thumb's width of space between your longest toe and the end of the shoe, as feet expand while running.
- **Try many shoes:** Visit a specialty running store for a fitting. Try on multiple pairs and go back to the ones that felt best.
- **Comfort rules:** If a shoe feels off when you first try it on, it likely won't feel better on a run.
- **Shop with a goal:** Consider distance (cushioning) vs. speed (weight and responsiveness).
- **Neutral vs. Stability:** Start with neutral shoes. Only move to stability shoes if you feel you want more support or if a doctor recommends them. Experts note that overpronation is an overused term and most people fall in the middle of the pronation bell curve.
- **Heel-to-toe drop:** Traditional shoes have 10-12mm drop. Low-drop shoes (0-4mm) are an alternative for those who prefer a more natural feel, but should be eased into to avoid injury.
- **Sizing:** Be flexible — every brand's sizing is different. Use your normal size as a starting point but don't be afraid to size up or down.
- **Gender-specific shoes:** Not necessarily needed, though women's shoes typically have narrower heels and different width options. Focus on comfort features rather than gendered marketing.
- **Rotate shoes:** Having multiple pairs can prevent overuse injuries and allow cushioning to recover between runs.
- **Return policy:** Check return policies, especially when buying online.

**Testing Methodology:** The team tested over 100 pairs of shoes over seven years, with testers putting at least 50 miles on each pair. They evaluated cushioning, responsiveness, ride, ground feel, fit over time, sole and upper support, weight, and style.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive Wirecutter guide on how to choose the best running shoes, updated in 2025. The guide is written by Seth Berkman and is based on insights from eight experts (including physical therapists, podiatrists, a running coach, and shoe company executives), extensive research, and over 5,500 miles of testing by the Wirecutter team since 2017.

**Key Recommendations:**

- **Best Neutral Running Shoes:** Asics Novablast 5 (women's $130, men's $130) — versatile daily trainers with noticeable propulsion and bounce. Also recommended: New Balance 1080v15 and Nike Pegasus 41.
- **Best Stability Running Shoes:** Saucony Guide 17 (women's $100, men's $110) — a drastically redesigned trainer with ample cushioning. Also recommended: New Balance Fresh Foam X 860v14.
- **Best Low-Drop Running Shoes:** Altra Escalante 4 (women's $130, men's $130) — a zero-drop shoe with good cushioning and a comfortable toe box.

**Key Buying Advice:**

- **Fit is paramount:** Aim for at least a thumb's width of space between your longest toe and the end of the shoe, as feet expand while running.
- **Try many shoes:** Visit a specialty running store for a fitting. Try on multiple pairs and go back to the ones that felt best.
- **Comfort rules:** If a shoe feels off when you first try it on, it likely won't feel better on a run.
- **Shop with a goal:** Consider distance (cushioning) vs. speed (weight and responsiveness).
- **Neutral vs. Stability:** Start with neutral shoes. Only move to stability shoes if you feel you want more support or if a doctor recommends them. Experts note that overpronation is an overused term and most people fall in the middle of the pronation bell curve.
- **Heel-to-toe drop:** Traditional shoes have 10-12mm drop. Low-drop shoes (0-4mm) are an alternative for those who prefer a more natural feel, but should be eased into to avoid injury.
- **Sizing:** Be flexible — every brand's sizing is different. Use your normal size as a starting point but don't be afraid to size up or down.
- **Gender-specific shoes:** Not necessarily needed, though women's shoes typically have narrower heels and different width options. Focus on comfort features rather than gendered marketing.
- **Rotate shoes:** Having multiple pairs can prevent overuse injuries and allow cushioning to recover between runs.
- **Return policy:** Check return policies, especially when buying online.

**Testing Methodology:** The team tested over 100 pairs of shoes over seven years, with testers putting at least 50 miles on each pair. They evaluated cushioning, responsiveness, ride, ground feel, fit over time, sole and upper support, weight, and style.
</summary>

Cushioned shoes provide both the comfort and support you need tacking on miles whether you’re a beginner or experienced runner. We take for granted what our bodies are capable of with just one step; the impact of running can range from 2.5 to even 5 times a person’s body weight with each foot strike. A cushioned [running shoe](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a19663621/best-running-shoes/) acts as a buffer for the constant pounding you subject your body too, and helps you cover faster thanks to that support.

At *Runner’s World*, our gear team tests all levels of foam in the crop of shoes that brands release every season. We’ve tested lightweight, daily trainers, [stability](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a20865766/best-stability-running-shoes/) shoes, and cushioned styles, to all *kinds* of cushioned running shoes which are specific to racing, everyday training, or recovery miles. Knowing foams only reveals a partial picture in finding your perfect cushioned pair. Thanks to our staff and team of run testers of various running levels, paces, and weekly mileage, we developed a list to help you find the best cushioned shoe that works for you and the types of workouts for your [training plan](https://www.runnersworld.com/training/a30911910/download-your-runners-world-training-plan/).

When I was on a call with Nike getting the rundown on the Structure Plus, I couldn’t get over this thought: Why would I ever choose the [Structure 26](https://www.kqzyfj.com/click-100815424-17049705?sid=ruw-xid-{xid}&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.nike.com%2Ft%2Fstructure-26-mens-road-running-shoes-M4sx9fru%2FHJ1102-100) now that there’s the Structure Plus?

The latter is lighter than the Structure 26 despite 4mm more cushioning in the midsole. Unlike the Structure 26, which only has ReactX, the Structure Plus has a top foam of ZoomX—the PEBA foam in Nike’s racing shoes. The geometry of the midsole is also wider to promote stability. The convex flat shape of the sidewall and denseness underneath the arch help with overpronation. And this stability feature isn’t intrusive. Neutral runners can also reap the benefits of a little more support and experience a high rebound ride with a layer of super foam.

One tester who suffers from [plantar fasciitis](https://www.runnersworld.com/health-injuries/a60027520/treatments-for-plantar-fasciitis/) appreciated the balanced cushioning of the Structure Plus, saying the shoe provided excellent support for her arch. Another tester, who overpronates and has a flat arch, was “pleasantly surprised” by the midfoot cushioning and stability of the shoe.

All this isn’t to say you shouldn’t consider the Structure 26. The trainer is a more accessible price at $140, and testers loved the shoe for its comfort, stability, and do-it-all workhorse ride.

On all other levels, the trainer is freakishly similar to the Clifton 11: same stack heights, same drop. The weight is just tenths of an ounce heavier but the responsive foam and aggressive Meta-Rocker make that tenths of extra weight an afterthought.

## What to Consider

### Stack Height

![](/_assets/design-tokens/fre/static/icons/arrow-right-regular.e879c19.svg)

Stack Height

Stack height refers to the height of the shoe’s footbed, midsole, and outsole in the heel and forefoot, i.e., the material between your foot and the ground. You’ll find in our modern-day realm of running footwear, it’s rare to have heel heights under 1.5 inches, much less 1. Most of the shoes on this list are above 35mm.   
It used to be that the higher the stack height, the heavier the shoe. Brands are now using airier foams that provide high rebound along with more height, support, and durability.

### Foams

![](/_assets/design-tokens/fre/static/icons/arrow-right-regular.e879c19.svg)

Foams

In 1975, [Brooks](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a20866339/best-brooks-running-shoes/) introduced an EVA (ethylene vinyl acetate) midsole in its Villanova shoe. Pre-EVA, comfort was second to practicality and performance. Rigid, tacky rubber was the norm in running shoes. EVA became the industry standard for its lightweight and shock absorption capabilities. Fast forward to today, and we’ve gone through a [super foam renaissance](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a64969945/secret-to-super-shoes/) where midsole foams are lighter, higher, and bouncier.

In the past 10 years, EVA has phased out in favor of supercritical foams, such as nitrogen-infused EVA, and PEBA foam. Stack heights have also gone above and beyond the World Athletics 40mm guideline, making some [super trainers “illegal”](https://www.runnersworld.com/gear/a46762781/super-trainers-illegal-running-shoes/) for competition—but darn fun to train in.

Midsole foams have a dual role in cushioning your feet as you run, protecting them from impact and absorbing shock. They also provide energy return, making your runs more energy-charged and responsive.

Types of foams used in midsoles include:

EVA: A foam that’s lightweight, soft, and reasonably durable, but doesn’t return as much energy as other materials.

TPU: Thermoplastic polyurethane is a durable material that returns more energy than EVA foam but also weighs more.

TPE: Thermoplastic elastomer foam combines the softness of a plastic-based foam with rubber for additional durability.

PEBA: Polyether block amide is an ultra-lightweight TPE variation that delivers exceptionally high energy return. It’s expensive and degrades relatively quickly, losing its springiness after 200 to 300 miles. Given that, it’s usually reserved for high-end racing shoes.

### Level of Cushioning

![](/_assets/design-tokens/fre/static/icons/arrow-right-regular.e879c19.svg)

Level of Cushioning

Today, cushioning comes in many flavors, making it all the more confusing to choose what kind you need. The short answer to “how much cushioning” is “enough to make running enjoyable so you can run longer.” Simply put, the level of cushioning is dependent on the wearer and the types of workouts they want to do in the shoe.   
You’ll likely want a more cushioned trainer for longer runs and for recovery runs after coming back from a race and easing back into training. Body weight, injury history, and footfall force are also things to consider.  
It *is* possible to overdo it on cushioning. A too soft shoe can spell trouble for some. If your foot doesn’t feel secure or if it feels like you’re running on Jello, then you might want to opt for a shoe with firmer cushioning.

Firm cushioning wrongly gets translated as cinderblock-hard. Soft, spongey cushioning, like the kind you find in the Megablast, may be too erratic for those with powerful turnover. A shoe like the Vomero 18, however, offers maximum cushioning with plenty of firm support.

### Shelf Life

![](/_assets/design-tokens/fre/static/icons/arrow-right-regular.e879c19.svg)

Shelf Life

It’s difficult knowing when to retire your shoes when the cushioning is super thick; it makes it hard to see when the foam is compressed or “packed out.” One way to check if the foam is wearing down is to remove the footbed, or sockliner, and check to see if there are indentations from your foot’s metatarsal heads in the forefoot of the shoe.   
Another way is to keep a log on how many miles you’ve run in the shoes. We generally recommend 300 to 500 miles, depending on the wearer. It’s important to change out your pair at least once or twice a year to prevent injury.

Runner's World published a guide to the best cushioned running shoes for base-building miles, injury-prone runners, and marathoners. The article explains that cushioned shoes act as a buffer against the impact of running (2.5-5 times body weight per foot strike). The gear team tested shoes across various categories with input from 300+ local runners.

**Shoes Reviewed:**

1. **Brooks Glycerin 23** - 10.6 oz (M), 8.7 oz (W), 8mm drop, 38mm heel. Features DNA Tuned foam with dual-cell technology. Formerly Brooks' most cushioned trainer. Personal favorite for long runs on hilly roads.

2. **New Balance Ellipse v1** - 9.6 oz (M), 7.7 oz (W), 8mm drop, 38mm heel. Retooled Fresh Foam X midsole described as "firm pillow" feel. Provides trampoline-like bounce.

3. **Adidas Hyperboost Edge** - 9 oz (M9.5), 7.8 oz (W7.5), 6mm drop, 45mm heel. PEBA-based Hyperboost Pro foam, Primeweave upper, Lighttraction outsole. Max-cushioned super trainer without a stiff plate.

4. **Nike Structure Plus** - 10.8 oz (M10), 8.2 oz (W7), 10mm drop, 42mm heel. Combines ZoomX top foam with ReactX, wider midsole geometry for stability. Testers with plantar fasciitis and flat arches praised its support.

5. **Altra Fwd Via 2** - 10.6 oz (M), 8.7 oz (W), 4mm drop, 37mm heel. Zero-drop intro shoe with rocker geometry, wide toebox suitable for bunions.

6. **Brooks Glycerin Flex** - 9.4 oz (M), 7.3 oz (W), 6mm drop, 36mm heel. Lightweight max-cushioned trainer with decoupled heel/forefoot for natural movement. Flexible but requires attention to form.

7. **Hoka Clifton Pro** - 10.4 oz (M), 8.5 oz (W), 8mm drop, 42mm heel (M). Supercritical foam midsole, aggressive Meta-Rocker. Elevated everyday trainer for strenuous workouts.

8. **Hoka Cielo X1 3.0** - 7.5 oz (M10), 6.2 oz (W8), 7mm drop, 37mm heel. Super shoe used by Alex Masai at Chicago Marathon (2:04:37, 3rd place). Half ounce lighter than previous version.

9. **Asics Megablast** - 7.6 oz (M), 6.6 oz (W), 8mm drop, 46mm heel. Massive cushioning (46mm heel, 38mm forefoot). Responsive but bulky; testers noted fatigue on long runs.

10. **Hoka Mafate X** - 12.1 oz (M10), 8.3 oz (W8), 7mm drop, 49mm heel. Trail shoe with PEBA midsole, pizza/taco-shaped lugs. Ideal for ultras and rocky terrain.

**What to Consider section covers:** Stack height (shoes above 35mm are common), Foams (EVA, TPU, TPE, PEBA types explained), Level of cushioning (dependent on workout type, injury history, body weight), and Shelf life (300-500 miles recommended; check for foam compression by removing sockliner).

All three shoes use a new midsole foam called FF Leap, which is an aliphatic thermoplastic polyurethane (ATPU) and seems to be the new “unlock” in materials. TPU has been used for more than a decade in shoes because it delivered better cushioning and energy return than the old EVA foam used for generations. The drawback: TPU is heavy. ATPU, though, is insanely soft, bouncy, and lively, but also extremely lightweight. Apparently, you can have your cake and eat it, too.

The Sky and Edge leverage this new foam along with a second layer of Turbo+, made from PEBA (sometimes called Pebax, a formulation branded by the polymer company Arkema), an old gold standard for super racers still used in a lot of performance running shoes. With both models, you’re getting a snappy shoe that works well at distances up to the marathon. A lot of us recreational runners find them better suited for shorter distances because the cushioning isn’t as squishy as some other super shoes.

The Ray takes the formula of the Edge and Sky but puts every bit of focus on weight; Asics tried to make it as light as possible. There was a time shoe manufacturers keyed in on weight for racers because studies showed that an additional 100 grams slows you by 1 percent. But modern foams have allowed shoe builders to largely think about “right weight” instead of light weight.

Asics was careful to say that the Ray is not necessarily a “pinnacle” product—not a superior racing shoe to the Edge or Sky. But it’s yet one more option for runners who seek the lightest possible racer.

The plate shape is closer in design to the Sky’s, but in this case, it covers only about 60 percent of the midsole length (to save weight, of course) and sits atop the slab of foam, thereby being best-suited for those who land midfoot to forefoot. This configuration works: If the plate was embedded in the foam, you’d end up with a stiffer, heavier midsole because of those glue joints. Here, the plate still allows you to harness as much of the cushioning and energy return from the foam as possible, while keeping the shoe malleable and lightweight.

With just one thick slab of FF Leap instead of two foams, is it too soft and untamable? Maybe. “The Ray gets kind of squirrelly at non-race speeds,” said Josh Davis, a former D1 runner. “If I knew I had great weather conditions and a course that was gentle on the corners, I could see the Ray’s lightness having an advantage for a long race.” The sentiment was shared by Trevor Conde, who has a marathon PR of 2:21: “The Ray is fast but comes at a cost because it’s just too squishy.”

What an age we live in, where a four-ounce shoe can feel too soft. A decade ago, a racing flat of the same weight would be teeth-rattling. If that one marshmallowy pair isn’t your flavor, there are two similarly suited versions that could give you what you need.*—J.D.*

Trevor Raab

Hoka is hitting its stride in the speed game with two legit super shoes in its current lineup. The Cielo X1 2.0 is a wild shoe with radical geometry and a bouncy response that’s kind of hard to tame. The Rocket X 3, however, is a more stable and firm speedster that will suit runners who seek the advantages of a modern racer with the predictability of a traditional running shoe—it was really well received by our testers.

The previous iteration ushered in PEBA foam and an insanely thin upper to deliver go-fast speeds with good underfoot softness. The foam remains the same in the newest version, and despite the silhouette looking chunkier, the shoe has managed to hold weight steadily. In our lab, we measured the heel stack height at 41 mm, which technically puts it over the limit allowed by World Athletics, but production tolerances are hard to control to such small measures, and the shoe has been given the okay by the sport’s governing body.

By widening the platform, Hoka delivers some extra torsional rigidity in the forefoot: It helps stabilize you at toe-off, allows you to take full advantage of the bouncy foam, and gives you a more propulsive stride.

Runner's World 2025 Winter Shoe Guide features 17 new running shoes tested by a wear-test team of over 250 runners who logged thousands of miles across 92 different models. The guide highlights how super shoe technology (bouncy foams, carbon plates) is trickling down to daily trainers.

**Key shoes covered:**

- **On Cloudultra Pro** ($260/$205 on sale): Trail racing shoe (9.7 oz, 6mm drop). Features Helion HF foam and H-shaped nylon Speedboard. Designed for UTMB terrain. Tested on 102-mile ZUT100 race. Breathable but thin upper vulnerable to abrasion. Good all-terrain grip but lacks bite on loose rock/sand.

- **Asics Megablast** ($225): Performance trainer (7.9 oz M, 8mm drop). Single layer of FF Turbo2 foam, no carbon plate. Versatile for easy jogs to track intervals. Originally conceived as a test for Superblast 3. Stripped-back, minimalist design.

- **Brooks Hyperion Elite 5** ($275/$200 on sale): Road racing shoe (7.0 oz M, 8mm drop). Softer foam than Elite 4 PB, smoother ride for marathon distances. Tester ran 2:42:47 at 2025 Boston Marathon in them. Grippy outsole. Low heel collar may cause slipping at slower speeds.

- **On Cloudsurfer Max** ($180): Max cushioning trainer (10.5 oz M, 6mm drop). 38mm heel with holes in foam for soft landings. Stiff out of box but loosens up. Forefoot praised as stable and bouncy. Fabric loops for lacing inconsistent.

- **Brooks Hyperion Max 3** ($200/$150 on sale): Super trainer (9.9 oz M, 6mm drop). Uses DNA Gold (PEBA) and DNA Flash v2 foams sandwiching a Pebax plate. 10mm taller stack than Hyperion 3. RapidRoll rocker technology. Described as softer, bouncier than previous version.

- **La Sportiva Prodigio Max** ($185): Trail shoe (10.9 oz M, 6mm drop). 37mm heel/31mm forefoot stack. Stable and predictable on technical terrain. Midsole wraps upper like a bumper. Snug, low-volume fit.

- **Asics Metaspeed Edge/Sky/Ray Tokyo** ($270-$300): Road racing shoes. All share same platform (39.5mm heel, 5mm drop). Sky for stride runners, Edge for cadence runners. New FF Leap (ATPU) foam. Ray is ultralight at 4.6 oz but described as "squirrelly" and "too squishy" at non-race speeds.

- **Brooks Cascadia 19** ($150): Trail shoe (10.7 oz M, 6mm drop). 19th iteration praised for comfort, traction, durability. Testers noted good balance of nimbleness and protection.

- **Mount to Coast T1** ($180): Trail shoe (9.3 oz M, 4mm drop). Features unique "Tunedfit Dual Lacing System" with split laces and drawstring pull tab. Vibram lugs good on pavement and mild gravel. Slippery on wet rocks.

- **Satisfy TheRocker** ($290): Trail shoe (9.9 oz M, 6mm drop). PEBA-and-EVA-blend midsole. Vibram Litebase/Megagrip outsole with round nubs inspired by RC car tires. Ripstop nylon upper (Rippy 66) is thin but tight-fitting.

- **Hoka Rocket X 3** ($250): Road racing shoe (8.0 oz M, 7mm drop). PEBA foam. 41mm heel stack. Carbon fiber plate with "winglet" for forefoot stability. Very grippy on wet roads.

- **New Balance FuelCell Rebel v5** ($145): Performance trainer (8.0 oz M, 6mm drop). PEBA and EVA blend midsole. More firm and responsive than v4. Minimal upper. Versatile for speedwork and daily training.

- **Skechers Aero Burst** (incomplete - price not listed): Max-cushioned trainer. Versatile at all paces, good cushioning with responsiveness. On the heavier side.

## Adidas Adizero Evo SL

![adidas adizero evo sl](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/adidas-adizero-evo-sl-68234a2c77085.jpg?resize=980:* "Adidas Adizero Evo SL")

Thomas Hengge

How good is this shoe? I think it’s so good that I actually purchased two more pairs for myself after first testing it, even though I have 170 pairs marked “active” in my training log. And, the day the Evo SL went on sale, I posted on Instagram calling it the shoe of the year. Folks at other brands texted to ask how I could make that declaration on February 1. My response: If there’s a better shoe for $150 or less that comes along this year, I’ll eat this shoe. So, stay tuned.)

What makes the Evo SL so great? Well, it mostly lies in the shoe’s simplicity and versatility. There’s just a single layer of outstanding foam, a stripped-down upper, and really not much else going on. It allows the shoe to shine—and it does so whether you’re jogging on a recovery day or turning your feet over quickly during an interval session. It truly is a do-it-all shoe, all at an affordable price.

The foam is the same Lightstrike Pro that Adidas uses in the Adios Pro 4 marathon racing shoe, which we also review in this guide. It’s a lightweight, less-dense foam that has strong cushioning properties and responsiveness. Unlike that super shoe, this one has no carbon-fiber rods (which Adidas used instead of a plate), but it does have a nylon shank in the midfoot for stability when you’re transitioning from heel to toe. That’s needed because the foam is quite soft and thick and would otherwise prove unstable. The heel stack height is 39mm, with most of that being foam.

Thomas Hengge

And that’s exactly what the Vomero does.

Nike recently reorganized its shoe lineup, dubbing the max-cushioned offerings as Vomero—daily trainers fall under the Pegasus badge, and stability is the domain of the Structure. And it delivers that through the addition of ZoomX foam, the same light and soft material Nike uses in its marathon racing shoes. Here, combined with a bottom layer of ReactX, the shoe offers a highly cushioned landing but still has responsiveness for long runs.

# Adidas Adizero Evo SL Review

Thanks to a premium midsole foam and no-nonsense design, this shoe pairs great cushioning with top-notch pace versatility

![gearlab tested logo](https://outdoorgearlab.b-cdn.net/images/gearlab_tested_v4_80w.png)

## Our Verdict

The **Adidas Adizero Evo SL** is ideal for runners who want a single shoe to accommodate a range of paces as they train for a race. It pairs Adidas' Lightstrike Pro midsole foam, which is highly protective and responsive, with a lightweight and straightforward build, creating a shoe that is a joy to wear and doesn't feel like it's holding you back when you tackle a fast workout. However, there are two key drawbacks. First, it's not a very stable shoe. Runners who value support will likely want to look elsewhere. Second, the Continental rubber outsole grips phenomenally well on pavement in all conditions, but really struggles on looser surfaces, making it less than ideal for those who run on gravel and other substrates. Overall, we highly recommend the Evo SL to anyone seeking a smooth, lightweight, and responsive option that doesn't compromise comfort.  

**REASONS TO BUY**

Excellent value

Premium midsole cushioning

Simple

Versatile

**REASONS TO AVOID**

Lacks stability

Poor grip on loose surfaces

  


## Our Analysis and Test Results

[![adidas adizero evo sl - the evo sl quickly became one of our all-time favorite shoes during...](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20200%20150'%2F%3E)](https://outdoorgearlab.b-cdn.net/photos/33/68/458318_6850_XXXL.webp)

The Evo SL quickly became one of our all-time favorite shoes during testing.   Credit: Nathaniel Bailey

  
 

### Comfort and Fit

  

The Evo SL features a solid upper, constructed with high-quality materials and no glaring issues. The fabric and mesh that come in contact with your foot are high-quality, with a soft and non-abrasive feel. We had no problems with rubbing or hotspots, although the non-gusseted tongue tended to migrate over the course of the run, which may cause rubbing issues on the top of the foot for some runners.

  

The heel cup on the Evo SL provides ample space without compromising heel retention. It isn't overly stiff or uncomfortable, and it didn't cause any abrasion on the back of our Achilles. Alternatively, the lacing system is a disappointment. First, the laces themselves are more difficult to use compared to competitors. They're thin and cinch down too easily, which can make it very difficult to untie knots. We hate these laces. The knot managed to snug itself impossibly tight on a wet run. They're so thin that we had a horrible time getting them undone with cold fingers. Second, it was easy to under-tighten the midfoot, which caused our feet to slip forward in the shoe. Finding the right lacing setup could take some experimentation.

[![adidas adizero evo sl - the evo sl tongue has an annoying tendency to roll when you put the...](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20200%20150'%2F%3E)](https://outdoorgearlab.b-cdn.net/photos/33/68/458307_22495_XXXL.webp)

The Evo SL tongue has an annoying tendency to roll when you put the shoe on, requiring a bit of wiggling and finger dexterity to fix.   Credit: Nathaniel Bailey

  

In terms of fit, the Evo SL is generous by Adidas' standards. The forefoot has plenty of room, and even borders on being too voluminous for runners with narrow forefeet. From there, the shoe tapers to an average width through the midfoot and heel. We think the width and shape of the shoe should suit most runners. Adidas appears to agree, as it fails to offer a wide version. The length of the shoe is about right, although runners with narrow feet will need to monitor their lacing to ensure their feet don't slide towards the front of the shoe.

[![adidas adizero evo sl - the evo sl cushioning works well for most runners, offering solid...](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20200%20150'%2F%3E)](https://outdoorgearlab.b-cdn.net/photos/33/68/458323_27314_XXXL.webp)

The Evo SL cushioning works well for most runners, offering solid heel and forefoot protection, along with a gentle rocker.   Credit: Nathaniel Bailey

  
 

### Cushioning

  

Cushioning is the standout feature of the Evo SL. The Adidas Lightstrike Pro features premium foam, providing excellent compression upon landing. The foam is highly resilient, meaning it returns a significant portion of the energy you put into it. There's a bit of bounce underfoot as you run, but it's not overstated. It's just bouncy enough to make you smile when you start your run, but it's not enough to be distracting or difficult to manage. Underfoot, the 39mm of cushioning is absorbent but a little firm. It feels like there is some structure under your foot. This resulted in a controlled feeling at easy paces, along with immediate responsiveness when the pace gets spicier. The more energy you put into the Evo, the more responsive it feels, and the softer the foam feels.

  

The foam is extremely protective on long runs. We felt less muscle soreness after an 18-mile progression run than we typically experience with non-race shoes. This is likely attributable to the midsole foam. In fact, many runners report feeling less soreness after *hard efforts* in “*super shoes*” (carbon-plated shoes that utilize premium, highly resilient midsole foams, such as Adidas' Lightstrike Pro). However, the relatively low weight (8.73 ounces in a US Men's 10.5) of the Evo SL probably helped as well.

[![adidas adizero evo sl - the evo sl rocker isn't hugely noticeable, and starts closer to the...](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20200%20150'%2F%3E)](https://outdoorgearlab.b-cdn.net/photos/31/92/440765_11491_XXXL.webp)

The Evo SL rocker isn't hugely noticeable, and starts closer to the midfoot, keeping it from feeling aggressive when running at slow paces.   Credit: Natalie Kafader

   
   

The Evo SL is a joy to run in. It's smooth rolling underfoot, featuring a subtle early-to-midfoot rocker and a 9mm heel-to-toe drop. Landings feel natural, and the shoe provides a noticeable boost as you roll forward on your foot. The main drawback here is the lack of stability. The Evo SL doesn't offer much lateral support, so runners with a history of pronation-related injuries or who value stability will likely want to look elsewhere.

[![adidas adizero evo sl - a phone flashlight easily shines through the upper of the evo...](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20200%20150'%2F%3E)](https://outdoorgearlab.b-cdn.net/photos/33/70/458571_4727_XXXL.webp)

A phone flashlight easily shines through the upper of the EVO, illustrating how lightweight and airy it truly is.   Credit: Nathaniel Bailey

  
 

### Breathability

  

The synthetic, engineered mesh of the Evo SL is very breathable, though not the best.

  

We experienced no issues with temperature regulation across a range of conditions, from 15 to 80°F. Our feet never felt cold nor overheated when running in the Evo, even for longer periods.

[![adidas adizero evo sl - the continental rubber outsole on the evo is tacky and thrives on...](data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8,%3Csvg%20xmlns%3D'http%3A%2F%2Fwww.w3.org%2F2000%2Fsvg'%20viewBox%3D'0%200%20200%20150'%2F%3E)](https://outdoorgearlab.b-cdn.net/photos/33/68/458312_28388_XXXL.webp)

The Continental rubber outsole on the Evo is tacky and thrives on pavement.   Credit: Nathaniel Bailey

  
 

### Traction

  

Continental rubber makes up the outsole of the Evo SL. It's a tacky compound that provides great grip on most smooth surfaces, but it struggles once things get loose or uneven.

  

We had no issues in conditions ranging from icy asphalt to hot, wet concrete. However, the lack of lugs is a significant drawback on looser surfaces, such as crushed gravel trails, where the shoe noticeably lacks grip as you push off the ground. While not designed as a trail running shoe, it would be beneficial for runners traversing various substrates to feel more confident on short stints over looser terrain, as they can be challenging to avoid.

## Should You Buy the Adidas Adizero Evo SL?

  

We believe the Evo SL should be at the top of your list if you're seeking a versatile shoe for serious training. It's comfortable and versatile enough to be a daily trainer for some runners, and a race shoe for others. Additionally, it offers great value, outperforming many shoes that cost significantly more.

## What Other Running Shoes Should You Consider?

  
 If versatility is at the top of your list, then the [New Balance Rebel v5](/reviews/shoes-and-boots/running-shoes-men/new-balance-fuelcell-rebel-v5) is a good choice, though it does fall short of the comfort and performance the Evo SL offers. On the other hand, if you like the idea of a versatile shoe but the Evo SL seems too performance-oriented, the [Asics Novablast 5](/reviews/shoes-and-boots/running-shoes-men/asics-novablast-5) is a top-performing shoe that many runners find extremely comfortable and fun.

args.summary:
The Adidas Adizero Evo SL is a lightweight, fast daily trainer reviewed by Runner's World UK (Ben) on May 29, 2025. Priced at £130, it's the entry-level shoe in the Adizero franchise but benefits from "trickle-down technology" from higher-end models like the Pro 4 and Takumi Sen.

**Key Specifications:**
- Weight: 244g (UK 8.5)
- Stack height: 39mm heel, 32mm forefoot (7mm drop)
- Foam: Light Strike Pro (responsive, lightweight)
- Upper: Breathable, less refined than premium models
- Thin, unpadded tongue; traditional Adidas lacing

**Performance:**
- Excels at faster training work (tempo, intervals, 5K/10K)
- Not ideal for slow easy runs, particularly for heavier or slower runners
- Slightly wider toe box than previous Adizero SL for better stability
- Mild rocker (less aggressive than race-day shoes like Pro 4)
- Secure fit with padded heel counter

**Cons:**
- Sizing runs small; reviewers unanimously recommend going up half a size
- Grip is compromised in wet conditions due to exposed Light Strike Pro foam on the outsole, which becomes slick when wet. The rubber layout lacks sufficient cutaways to prevent foam contact with wet ground.

**Overall Verdict:** A unanimous tester recommendation as a great shoe at a great price point (£130)—comfortable, cushioned, responsive, and lively for faster running. The main drawbacks are sizing and wet-weather grip.

## Who should buy

Despite its limited early release, we managed to buy a pair of the Adizero EVO SL, and after dissecting it and testing every detail, we recommend it for:

* Beginners wanting a do-it-all shoe for training and racing that offers reliable performance at an unbeatable price.
* Anyone seeking a speedy, durable and fun training partner.
* Runners who dislike carbon plates but crave world-class performance and grip.
* Those searching for a versatile shoe with premium foam without breaking the bank.

## Who should NOT buy

The EVO SL impressed us in many ways, but we think it’s not the best choice for runners with stability concerns. Its narrow midsole and lack of support make it unsuitable for those needing even mild support. In our view, a better alternative would be the [ASICS Superblast 2](https://runrepeat.com/asics-superblast-2), which offers a more stable platform and an improved upper—addressing one of the EVO SL’s weakest points.

 

Additionally, we know this shoe won’t satisfy runners seeking the sensation of a plate. The EVO SL is designed for a more natural ride. For those desiring a plated trainer, we recommend the [PUMA Deviate Nitro 3](https://runrepeat.com/puma-deviate-nitro-3) or the [Saucony Endorphin Speed 4](https://runrepeat.com/saucony-endorphin-speed-4).

Finally, the limited early release by adidas might make it impossible to spend your money on this shoe. If it’s unavailable but you’re seeking a similar experience, we believe the [New Balance FuelCell Rebel v4](https://runrepeat.com/new-balance-fuelcell-rebel-v4) or the [Nike Pegasus Plus](https://runrepeat.com/nike-pegasus-plus) offer the closest running feel to the EVO SL, both being widely available worldwide.

The midsole is where the magic truly happens in this shoe. Lightstrike Pro ranks as one of our favorite superfoams, showcasing an extraordinary blend of durability and performance that, in our experience, still remains unmatched. The Adizero EVO SL basically defies its $150 price point with a full 100% Lightstrike Pro midsole, delivering the same propulsive, spring-like ride that anyone familiar with this foam would expect. ### Lightstrike Pro

When adidas first announced this shoe, it surprised everyone—especially because they claimed the Lightstrike Pro foam was exactly the same used in the [adidas Adizero Adios Pro 3](https://runrepeat.com/adidas-adizero-adios-pro-3), their high-end marathon racer. That’s quite rare in a $150 shoe!

 

Here’s why: some brands engage in what we see as borderline dark marketing. Take FuelCell from [New Balance](https://runrepeat.com/catalog/new-balance-running-shoes) as an example: in the Rebel v4, it’s 20% PEBA and 80% EVA, resulting in good-but-not-great energy return. But in the [Elite v4](https://runrepeat.com/new-balance-fuel-cell-super-comp-elite-v-4), it’s 100% PEBA—making it incredibly bouncy and responsive.

Yet both shoes carry the same “FuelCell” branding, and most runners don’t realize they’re getting vastly different foams. That’s where we step in.

When we got the EVO SL—despite its extremely limited release—we wasted no time. Cutting a chunk of foam and examining it under the microscope, we confirmed it’s the same state-of-the-art Lightstrike Pro found in the Adios Pro 3, offering amazing durability and energy return. The minor differences between the two images are because of the shelf life of our Adios Pro 3 pair and its usage.

![adidas Adizero EVO SL Genuine Lightstrike Pro](https://cdn.runrepeat.com/storage/gallery/product_content/40586/adidas-adizero-evo-sl-genuine-lightstrike-pro-22259773-main.jpg)

### Plate

One of the unique features of the EVO SL is its plate-free design—an interesting choice that we found enhances versatility, making it suitable for a wide range of paces, from easy runs to track intervals.

However, we discovered a plastic shank embedded in the midfoot, offering just enough stability to balance the ride of the full-length, ultra-bouncy foam. It’s similar to Nike’s Streakfly design but positioned closer to the foot.

Given the short tongue on the EVO SL, we found that a traditional runner's knot at the top eyelet might create uncomfortable pressure on the instep. However, as you can see, we did fine with a regular knot.

Nonetheless, we were generally pleased with the lacing system, which incorporates punched eyelets reminiscent of the Evo 1’s design. But we need to point out one persistent issue with adidas—the laces are frustratingly subpar, a recurring problem across all Adizero shoes that, unfortunately, still hasn’t been addressed in 2024.

## adidas Adizero EVO SL Review Summary

This is a comprehensive lab and field test review of the adidas Adizero EVO SL running shoe, published on RunRepeat by expert reviewer Carlos Sánchez. The review is based on the site's methodology 2.5 and includes extensive lab testing across durability, cushioning, breathability, stability, and more.

### Overall Verdict

The EVO SL receives an excellent overall score of 94/100 (Daily running 90, Tempo 92, Race 85, Stability 77). The review describes it as having the potential to "transform the running shoe industry" due to its exceptional value-to-performance ratio.

**Key Features:**
- **Midsole:** 100% Lightstrike Pro superfoam (same as the Adios Pro 3 marathon racer, confirmed via lab testing)
- **Outsole:** Continental rubber (world-class grip)
- **Weight:** 7.9 oz (223g) — extremely light for a daily trainer
- **Stack:** 36.1mm heel / 28.1mm forefoot (lab measured; brand states 38.5mm/32mm)
- **Drop:** 8.0mm lab measured (brand states 6.5mm)
- **Price:** ~$150 (MSRP) — notably affordable for the specs

**Pros:**
- 100% Lightstrike Pro superfoam
- Exceptional value-to-performance ratio
- Low weight (7.9oz/223g)
- Ultra-breathable upper
- Unmatched versatility (handles easy runs to races)
- Agile, fun ride without a carbon plate
- Striking EVO 1-inspired design

**Cons:**
- Poor-quality laces
- Short, non-gusseted tongue
- Low toebox durability (1/5 score)
- Not suitable for runners needing stability support

### Cushioning & Performance

- **Shock absorption:** 147 SA (heel) — rivals max-cushioned models, well above the 131 SA average
- **Energy return:** 74.3% — top-tier bounce, vastly exceeding the 58.6% average
- **Midsole softness:** 43.5 AC (firmer than average 35.7 AC, but springy)
- **Cold weather performance:** Only 13% change in softness after freezing (average is 22%), meaning consistent performance in winter
- **Rocker:** Smooth, gradual forefoot rocker (60% geometry, same as Adios Pro Evo 1) for natural transitions
- **No plate:** Uses a plastic shank in the midfoot instead of a full-length carbon plate, offering a more natural, versatile ride

### Fit & Sizing

- **Size:** True to size
- **Toebox width:** 97.5mm at widest (wider than average 95.2mm), but tapers to 71.6mm at big toe (narrower than 73.2mm average) — racer-inspired performance fit
- **Toebox height:** 28.1mm (adequate)
- **Widths available:** Normal and Wide

### Durability

- **Toebox durability:** 1/5 (poor, due to ultra-breathable single-layer mesh)
- **Heel padding:** 5/5 (excellent)
- **Outsole durability:** Excellent — only 0.6mm wear (average is 1.1mm), despite the outsole being only 1.6mm thick (half the average)
- **Outsole rubber:** Continental forefoot patch with cutouts + Clear Rubber heel pieces

### Stability

- **Not a stability shoe** — suited only for neutral runners
- **Torsional rigidity:** 4/5 (stiffer than average daily trainers due to the midfoot shank)
- **Heel counter:** 3/5 (moderate stiffness)
- **Midsole width:** 116.3mm forefoot (slightly above average), 87.3mm heel (narrower than average 91.2mm) — narrow heel is typical Adizero DNA
- **Heel bevel:** Aggressive design to help guide heel strikers

### Breathability

- **Breathability:** 76 BR (above average 72 BR) — good heat and moisture management
- **Drying potential:** 43% (below average 53%) — the upper is a weak point

### Who Should Buy

- Beginners wanting a do-it-all shoe for training and racing at an unbeatable price
- Runners seeking a speedy, durable, and fun training partner
- Runners who dislike carbon plates but want world-class performance and grip
- Those wanting premium foam without breaking the bank

### Who Should NOT Buy

- Runners with stability concerns (narrow midsole, lack of support)
- Those wanting a plated, stiff super-shoe feel
- Runners who cannot find the shoe due to its limited early release

| Breathability | 76 BR | 72 BR |
| Toebox durability | 1/5 | 2.6/5 |
| Heel padding durability | 5/5 | 3.4/5 |
| Outsole durability | 0.6 mm wear | 1.1 mm wear |
| Flexibility | 9.8N | 15.5N |

- Top pick in best running shoes
- Top pick in best running shoes for plantar fasciitis

- Top 3% in adidas running shoes

## Our verdict

* Daily running 93
* Tempo 91
* Race 86
* Stability 93

The ASICS Superblast 3 had a tough mission: improving a super trainer that already sells incredibly well despite its high price. To achieve that, ASICS delivered meaningful upgrades, as we found in the lab a softer, more protective ride with even better grip and lower weight. We really liked how it keeps its stable, versatile feel even with the much plusher FF Leap foam. It's true that the price has gone up and the upper handles airflow in a somewhat unusual way, but even so, this is clearly the best Superblast to date.

### Pros

* Exceptional shock absorption
* Improved energy return
* Softer FF Leap foam
* Lightweight despite maximal stack height
* Best traction we've seen to date
* Solid durability from top to bottom
* Keeps a very stable underfoot feel
* Versatile for multiple paces

### Cons

* FF Blast+ limits energy return
* Unexpected price bump
* Limited toebox breathability

### Awards

## Who should buy

In our opinion, the ASICS Superblast 3 shines for runners that:

* Enjoyed version 1 and 2 but found them a bit too firm. This new version delivers a much softer ride!
* Want a super trainer that blends bounce, stability, durability, and strong grip in a single package.
* Run high mileage and need maximum protection for muscles and joints while still enjoying an impressively lightweight shoe.
* Are willing to pay a premium price to get top-tier technology even for daily training.

## Who should NOT buy

The ASICS Superblast 3 comes slightly short of the most energetic super trainers, and that happens because [ASICS](https://runrepeat.com/catalog/asics-running-shoes) still included FF Blast+ in the lower section of the midsole. If maximum bounce is what you are looking for, take a look at the [ASICS Megablast](https://runrepeat.com/asics-megablast).

 

We also think that the high price of the Superblast 3 can be a deal-breaker for many runners. Luckily, there are now more affordable super trainers like the [adidas Adizero EVO SL](https://runrepeat.com/adidas-adizero-evo-sl) or the [Saucony Endorphin Azura](https://runrepeat.com/saucony-endorphin-azura) that deliver top-tier bounce and shock absorption at a very reasonable price.

## Cushioning

### Shock absorption

The biggest update in the Superblast 3 comes from FF Leap, a soft A-TPU foam that replaces the firmer FF Turbo+. And it is in terms of shock absorption where this change makes a real difference.

In our lab test, we found that the ASICS Superblast 3 displayed world-class levels with 154 SA in the heel and 153 SA in the forefoot. Yes, you read it right: at the time of this review, this is the shoe that provides more protection in the forefoot, even more than the [Nike Vomero Premium](https://runrepeat.com/nike-vomero-premium)!

### Midsole softness

Note: Low measurement: softer. High measurement: firmer.

While the SB1 and SB2 felt fairly similar underfoot, the SB3 delivers a noticeably different sensation with every step. This is because ASICS has moved away from the firmer top layer of PEBA foam used in previous versions (FF Turbo / FF Turbo+) and introduced the ultra-plush FF Leap compound.

## Breathability

### Breathability test

ASICS keeps evolving the Superblast upper with every version. The first generation was clearly race-inspired, borrowing ideas from the MOTIONWRAP upper seen in the Metaspeed series, while the second version focused much more on structure and comfort.

 

This third version is lighter than its predecessor, but once again introduces a new material with a woven mesh. The challenge for some runners is that ventilation is mostly concentrated in the tongue, as ASICS added oversized ventilation holes there but skipped them in the toebox.

 

For this reason, we rated the Superblast 3 with moderate breathability, as we believe that airflow in the toebox is essential for those running in hot climates. The SB3 directs most of the ventilation toward the tongue, but since it sits so close to the instep, there is limited space for air to circulate effectively.

The mesh looks impressive under the microscope and feels more premium than a standard engineered mesh upper.

In terms of comfort, this version is also an upgrade. It features improved and more generous padding in the heel area, which stands out immediately, especially considering how lightweight the shoe remains.

## Stability

### Lateral stability test

One of the features that made the Superblast a groundbreaking shoe in 2022 was its ability to combine a maximal stack height with excellent stability. Naturally, switching the midsole to the ultra-soft FF Leap foam, along with a softer version of FF Blast+, could have challenged that balance. However, ASICS had a clever solution.

The Superblast 3 slightly adjusts the midsole design by adding more FF Blast+ under the arch, helping reduce excessive compression from FF Leap in that area for runners with pronation tendencies. The rest of the usual methods employed by ASICS are still present, like the raised midsole sidewalls in the heel and midfoot areas.

### Tongue padding

ASICS has fully revamped the lacing system and opted this time for the so-called "lace in lace" setup. It's a unique design, as it features an elastic cord that runs across the entire eyelet chain while being stitched to form the eyelets. The top half uses punched eyelets too, while the bottom relies only on this cord-based structure.

It is excellent for pressure control, but long-term durability remains an open question. However, ASICS seems confident, as this is not the first shoe where we have seen it in the lab, with the [Trabuco 14](https://runrepeat.com/asics-trabuco-14) featuring a similar design.

The tongue keeps the same low thickness seen in recent ASICS shoes, which has been working well for the brand. It helps keep weight low, although for those seeking a more plush step-in feel, having only 1.9 mm of padding may feel underwhelming.

# ASICS Superblast 3 Review Summary

The ASICS Superblast 3 is a premium super trainer reviewed by Carlos Sánchez on RunRepeat, evaluated using methodology 2.3. It received an overall score of 94/100 (Superb) with category scores: Daily Running 93, Tempo 91, Race 86, and Stability 93.

## Key Upgrades & Features
- **New FF Leap foam** replaces the firmer FF Turbo+ as the top layer, delivering a softer, plusher ride
- **FF Blast+** remains as the secondary/carrier foam, but is now softer (37.0 AC vs previous version)
- **Weight**: Reduced to 8.3 oz (235g) — down from 8.9 oz (252g) in Superblast 2
- **World-class shock absorption**: 154 SA (heel) and 153 SA (forefoot) — best forefoot protection tested to date
- **Energy return**: 67.8% (+2.3% vs Superblast 2, +3.5% vs original)
- **Traction**: Outstanding 1.05 score — the highest rated running shoe in this metric
- **Stack height**: 45.8 mm heel / 37.7 mm forefoot (8.1 mm drop)
- **Midsole softness**: 22.8 AC (much softer than average of 35.7 AC)
- **Cold performance**: Only 1% change in softness after freezing (average is 22%)

## Pros
Exceptional shock absorption, improved energy return, softer FF Leap foam, lightweight despite maximal stack, best traction seen to date, solid durability, stable underfoot feel, versatile for multiple paces.

## Cons
FF Blast+ limits energy return potential, unexpected price bump, limited toebox breathability.

## Stability & Durability
- Wide midsole base (120.7 mm forefoot, 95.0 mm heel)
- Torsional rigidity: 18.2 Nm (stiff, no carbon plate)
- Heel counter stiffness: 4/5
- Outsole durability: Excellent (0.5 mm wear vs 1.1 mm average)
- Breathability: Moderate (3/5) — ventilation concentrated in tongue

## Fit & Specs
- True to size
- Toebox: Narrower than average (71.6 mm)
- Semi-gusseted tongue with 1.9 mm padding
- Extended heel collar
- Price: ₹24,380 (increased from previous version)
- Release date: March 1, 2026
- Terrain: Road | Neutral arch support | Suitable for heel and forefoot strikers

## Who Should Buy
Runners who enjoyed v1/v2 but found them too firm; those wanting a super trainer blending bounce, stability, durability, and grip; high-mileage runners needing maximum protection; those willing to pay premium.

## Who Should NOT Buy
Runners seeking maximum bounce (consider ASICS Megablast instead); budget-conscious runners (more affordable alternatives exist like adidas Adizero EVO SL or Saucony Endorphin Azura).

## Verdict
The Superblast 3 is described as "clearly the best Superblast to date" with meaningful upgrades including a softer, more protective ride, better grip, and lower weight. It maintains its stable, versatile feel even with the plusher foam.

However, the Superblast 3 is a versatile "everything shoe" suitable for easy runs, threshold runs, long runs, hill repeats, and even some racing. The shoe officially drops on March 1, 2026. Durability of the new FF Leap foam on top is a potential concern, though the bottom FF Blast foam should be very durable.

# Asics Superblast 3 Review: The Blast Samurai

 ![asics superblast 3 - feature](https://believeintherun.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/asics-superblast-3-feature-.jpg)

### In This Article

## What You Need To Know
